proposals.reason: Common on good and fine-dining American menus for octopus, shrimp, scallops and whole fish: cooked on a ripping-hot flat steel plate, Spanish style, so the food takes a hard, even crust with no grill marks and no smoke, and delicate things do not fall through a grate. The near neighbors are Seared (L1) and Grilled (L1), and the server has to tell the three apart. Unchallenged; the most frequent of the section's new words. Specialist fine-dining vocabulary that needs explaining: Sous Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that grilled? What does plancha mean?
proposals.menuLine: Octopus à la Plancha, fingerling potatoes, salsa verde, smoked paprika

proposals.reason: A fine-dining showpiece verb (whole branzino for two, celery root, beets, where menus also print it Salt-Roasted or Salt-Crusted, which the card should carry as aliases): sealed in a crust of coarse salt and egg white and baked, so it steams in its own moisture and comes out seasoned and tender, not salty; often cracked open tableside. Nothing in the deck reaches it (Brined and Cured are salt, but different acts), and the guest's fear that it will be too salty is the question every server fields. Unchallenged. Fine-dining vocabulary that takes a sentence: Sous Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: Won't it be way too salty? Do we eat the crust?
proposals.menuLine: Salt-Baked Branzino for Two, fennel, Castelvetrano olives, Meyer lemon

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list. The fine-dining word for glazed, printed on new American menus for duck, pork belly and quail: brushed with a glaze in layers as it roasts until the surface sets glossy, dark and slightly sticky, the skin underneath rendered crisp. The deck has no Glazed card, and its nearest neighbor, Caramelized (L1), is a different act (browning sugar, not building a coat), so the guest's question has nowhere else to land. Opaque to guests, frequent on menus, one clear sentence to explain: Sous Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that sweet? Is the skin going to be crispy?
proposals.menuLine: Lacquered Duck Breast, turnips, black plum, five-spice jus

proposals.reason: The section's first Level IV card, in one of the five sections that held none. The rare specialist verb of modern American fine dining (Koji-Aged Ribeye, Koji-Cured Pork Collar, which the card should carry as an alias, Koji-Aged Carrots): meat or vegetables coated in koji, rice grown with the Aspergillus oryzae mold that makes miso and sake, whose enzymes tenderize and build deep savory, nutty flavor in days, mimicking weeks of dry-aging. Its near neighbor is Dry-Aged (L2, Language), and the deck has no card for koji under any term, though Miso (L2, Pantry) can point to it. A senior server must own it because the honest answer involves the word mold and has to be given calmly and correctly. Unchallenged. Rare and specialist: Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is koji? Is that a mold? Is it safe to eat?
proposals.menuLine: Koji-Aged Prime Ribeye, bone marrow, charred onion, black garlic jus

dispositions.reason: The challenger is right on the standard's own signals. Butter-poached lobster is on the menu at every upscale American steakhouse, so a server meets it nightly by the second week; the explanation is one sentence (cooked gently in melted butter, so it stays soft and rich, never fried); it is the confusable pair with Poached (L1), which is exactly what Level II holds; and its sibling Confit already sits at Level II. Beurre monté is the cook's reason, not the guest's, and does not lift the word a level. Moved to Level II, which puts it outside this Level III and IV roster, so it is dropped here and should be handed to a Level II pass for Cooking Methods, where it is a strong card.

Added at Level 3. Frequent on new American and fine-dining menus for duck, pork belly and quail, opaque to guests, and the deck has no Glazed card and no neighbor that reaches it (Caramelized is browning sugar, not building a coat). It outranks the other missing words on menu frequency and on how far it sits from any existing card.

A real Level III word and the first alternate for this section, but the roster holds four and it is outranked. Its near neighbors already sit in the deck at Level I: Grilled is taught as cooked over glowing coals and Smoked as flavored by smoldering wood, so the guest's question (is it burnt, is there ash on it) is one sentence away from an existing card, where Lacquered and Salt-Baked have no card that reaches them. If the deck later wants a fifth word here, this is it, with Coal-Roasted and Ash-Roasted as aliases.

Real on new American menus but seasonal (watermelon, melon, cucumber in summer) and reachable from an existing card: Sous Vide (L2) already teaches vacuum-sealing, and compression is the same bag and machine used on raw fruit, so the answer to what compressed means is a sentence that card can carry. Below the cap on frequency and on distance from the deck.

Does not belong at Level III or IV. By the challenger's own steakhouse test, the one that moved Butter-Poached, a word printed on steakhouse menus for tomahawks and thick chops and explained in one sentence is Level II. It is also more a book and blog word than a menu word (the technique's home is food writing, and most kitchens that use it do not print it), and the roster prefers menu words. Pan-Roasted (L2) already teaches sear plus oven, and the guest's real question, is it cooked all the way through, is answered there in the other order. A Level II pass may take it as a confusable pair with Pan-Roasted.

A legitimate Level IV word and the second alternate for this section, but the roster holds four and Koji-Aged is the stronger Level IV: koji has spread across modern American menus while hay-smoking stays rare, and Smoked (L1) is a close neighbor that a server can lean on (a different fuel, a sweet grassy smoke, no hay on the plate). If the deck wants a second Level IV for Cooking Methods, take this next, with Hay-Roasted as an alias.

challenges.because: This is not fine-dining vocabulary, it is steakhouse vocabulary. Butter-poached lobster tail is on the menu at every upscale steakhouse in America, chain or independent (Capital Grille, Del Frisco's, Ocean Prime, and every surf-and-turf add-on), so a Level II server meets it nightly by the second week, not once a season. It is the confusable pair with Poached (L1), which is exactly what the standard says Level II holds, and the explanation is one sentence: cooked gently in melted butter, so it is soft and rich, never fried. Its sibling Confit (cooked submerged in fat) sits at Level II already; beurre monté is the cook's reason, not the guest's, and does not raise the word a level.

missing: Ember-Roasted [3] (Coal-Roasted, Ash-Roasted: vegetables and whole fish cooked directly in or on the coals or the ash; the fine-dining near neighbor of Roasted and Grilled, and guests ask whether it is burnt and whether there is ash on it)

Lacquered [3] (duck, pork belly, quail brushed with a glaze and cooked until the surface sets glossy and dark; the fine-dining word for glazed, and guests ask whether it is sweet and whether the skin is crisp)

Compressed [3] (fruit or vegetable vacuum-sealed so the flesh is pressed dense, translucent and intensified, compressed watermelon and compressed melon on new American menus every summer; guests ask what compressed means and whether it is cooked)

Reverse-Seared [3] (thick steak or chop brought up slowly in a low oven or water bath, then seared hard at the end; printed on steakhouse menus for tomahawks and thick chops, guests ask what it means and whether it is cooked all the way through; the near neighbor of Pan-Roasted (L2) run in the other order)

Hay-Smoked [4] (Hay-Roasted: meat, fish or butter cooked or finished over smoldering hay for a sweet grassy smoke; rare, fine-dining showpiece, often brought to the table under a cloche, and guests ask whether it is safe and whether they are eating hay)
sections.note: Four proposals, three at III and one at IV, since Cooking Methods held nothing above Level II. Runners-up not proposed, all checked against everyCard: Binchotan-Grilled (IV, Japanese white charcoal; frequent at izakaya and on some tasting menus but less common than Koji-Aged on American menus, a fair alternate if a second IV is wanted); Hay-Smoked (IV, Smoked at L1 already carries the act, and it reads as a variant); Nage / à la Nage (IV, but it is a court-bouillon broth served as sauce, so it belongs to Sauces or Preparations, not the verbs); Fricassée (III, a white stew and a dish form, so it sits with Ragout and Cassoulet in Preparations); Reverse-Seared (III on steakhouse menus but reads as a variant of Seared). The brief's two method candidates (Wok Hei, Grilling vs. Barbecue vs. Smoking) are book essays, not menu words, so none of the proposals carries a lexiconSlug. En Papillote and Meunière were considered and rejected because Preparations already teaches them.

proposals.reason: The stomach lining of beef (honeycomb tripe), scrubbed and simmered for hours until tender and mild, is the organ a server at an Italian-American or Mexican-leaning good restaurant meets most: trippa alla Fiorentina, trippa alla Romana, menudo. A specialist product that takes an honest sentence to a nervous guest (what part it is, that it is long-cooked, that it eats soft and takes on its sauce), which is the section's blurb exactly. Level 3 because it is on menus often enough that a Sous Chef-level server should own it; not a variant of Beef Tongue or Bone Marrow, the deck's other beef organs. No Lexicon candidate holds it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What exactly is tripe, and is it chewy or does it taste like the stomach?
proposals.menuLine: Trippa alla Fiorentina, San Marzano tomato, pecorino, mint, grilled bread

proposals.reason: The heart is the offal that arrives most often at nose-to-tail and wood-fire restaurants today: grilled duck hearts on a skewer, beef heart anticuchos on Peruvian menus, chicken hearts at yakitori counters. It is a working muscle rather than a gland, so it eats like a dense dark-meat steak and not like liver, which is the one sentence that reassures a wary guest and which the Chicken Liver card cannot supply. Common enough on fine-dining menus for Level 3. The card names beef and chicken heart as aliases and gives gizzards one line (the other working-muscle organ, firmer, confit on the bistro salad), so the challenger's Gizzards point is met without a fifth card.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is heart chewy, and does it taste strong like liver?
proposals.menuLine: Grilled Duck Hearts, salsa verde, pickled shallot, grilled sourdough

proposals.reason: The two small ovals of dark meat set in the hollows of the backbone above the thigh, the sot-l'y-laisse of classical French cooking, now printed on tasting menus as their own course. Rare, deeply classical, and actively confusable with the deck's Oysters card in the fish section, so a senior server must own it rather than guess, and must be able to tell a shellfish-allergic guest plainly that there is no shellfish in it. Level 4 by the standard (Ballotine, Acquerello). The deck teaches no chicken part under any term; Duck Breast/Magret does not reach it. A bird's cut, so this section, where Duck Breast already lives.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is there actual oyster in this, or what part of the chicken is a chicken oyster?
proposals.menuLine: Chicken Oysters, morels, vin jaune, spring garlic, brioche crumb

proposals.reason: The Muscovy x Pekin hybrid duck raised for American foie gras (Hudson Valley, La Belle), whose large, deep-red breast is the magret; fine-dining menus print the breed on both the breast and the seared foie, and a guest reads it as a farm or a French place. The Duck Breast card teaches the cut and its alias Magret but not the breed; Foie Gras teaches the liver but not the bird. This card also carries the contrast a server actually gets asked for: Pekin (Long Island) is the smaller, milder bird most duck breast comes from and is not Peking duck the dish, and brand names such as Rohan and Liberty are farms' proprietary ducks, not places. A breed word that is rare, specialist and needs a precise explanation is Level 4 by the standard (Washed Rind, Banyuls). Poultry, so this section.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does Moulard mean, is it a farm, a place, or a kind of duck?
proposals.menuLine: Moulard Duck Breast, cherries, hakurei turnip, duck jus

dispositions.reason: A true Level 4 offal word and the section's honest fifth: rognons de veau appear on a handful of French bistro menus in America and almost nowhere else, so on the standard's first signal (how often it is on menus) it loses to all four kept words, and the section is capped at four. If the owner lifts the cap, this is the first word to add, at Level 4, and the smell question is the card's opening sentence.

The bistro-salad and yakitori uses are real, but the sentence a server needs (a working muscle, dense, not gland-like, nothing like liver) is the Duck Hearts sentence with one word changed (firmer). The Duck Hearts card now gives gizzards a line by name, so the deck teaches the word without spending one of four cards on it. The fried-gizzard route is a Southern staple and the deck's Southern section was removed by the owner.

Not a variant of Chicken Liver, agreed, but by the standard it is a Level 2 word: foie de veau with bacon and onions is common at a good bistro and needs one sentence (a different animal, sliced and seared pink, milder than beef liver). This roster places only Levels 3 and 4. The Chicken Liver card already carries the iron-rich, silky-unless-overcooked sentence a guest's 'is it strong?' question turns on. Flag it for a Level 2 pass.

Rare, and rare in the wrong way: it appears on American menus almost only in December, as a roast for the table, so it is a word met in books and at holidays rather than on the working menu, and the standard prefers menu words. The gentle explanation (a rooster castrated young, so it grows large, fat and tender) belongs in the Poussin card as the other end of the same bird's life, not in one of the section's four new cards.

A proprietary brand (D'Artagnan's), and the challenger's description is wrong: Rohan is a cross of Heritage Mallard and Pekin, not a Pekin-Moulard cross. The deck should not spend a card on one distributor's trademark; the Moulard card now says plainly that Rohan and Liberty are farms' proprietary ducks, not places, which is the whole of what a guest needs.

The Peking-versus-Pekin confusion is a confusable pair, which the standard places at Level 2 (Hanger Steak, Branzino, Macaron), so it is out of this roster's scope on its own. The contrast that matters on a fine-dining floor (Pekin/Long Island: smaller, milder, most duck breast; Moulard: large, red, the foie bird) is now written into the Moulard card, where a guest actually raises it.

In trade and menu usage venison covers deer, elk and antelope, and most American elk is sold and served exactly as the Venison card describes it: deep red, very lean, loin served rare to medium rare. The guest's question (gamier than venison?) is answered inside that card with one line (elk is the milder and larger of the two). Not a new word the deck fails to teach, so it does not earn one of four cards.

A genuine gap, and the challenger already concedes the level: pappardelle al cinghiale and boar ragu are on most Italian-American menus, which by the standard is Level 2 (common at a good restaurant, needs a sentence: a leaner, darker, sweeter pork with a faint wild edge). This roster places only Levels 3 and 4; flag Wild Boar as the section's first Level 2 addition.

Belongs in this section beside Escargot and would be a fair Level 3, but on American menus it is rarer than every one of the four kept words (a few French bistros and Cajun rooms), and the section is capped at four. The nervous-guest sentence (tastes between chicken and a mild white fish, eaten off the bone) can ride as a line in the Escargot card, which already holds the 'what is this animal and will I like it' job. Second in line after Veal Kidneys if the cap lifts.

A gastropub and tapas word with a real texture question, but it is head meat and cartilage rather than an organ, so it sits at the edge of this section rather than its center, and its menu frequency is below Tripe, the kept card that does the same job of putting a wary guest at ease about a strange texture. Capped out at four; if the owner wants a fifth Level 3 here, Frog Legs and Veal Kidneys come first.

missing: Veal Kidneys [4] (rognons de veau on French bistro menus; the one organ a guest asks about the smell of, so it needs the honest sentence the blurb calls for; nothing in the deck touches kidney)

Gizzards [3] (confit gizzards on the bistro salad, fried gizzards on Southern menus, sunagimo at the yakitori counter; a working muscle like heart but a different bite, so its own card, not a line buried inside Duck Hearts)

Calf's Liver [3] (foie de veau on bistro menus, seared and served pink with onions and bacon; not a variant of Chicken Liver, a different animal, a different cut and a different way of eating it, and the guest's question is whether it is strong)

Capon [4] (roast capon at holiday and Italian-American menus; a castrated rooster, which is exactly the explanation a server must have ready and phrase gently; nothing in the deck holds it and Poussin is the opposite end of the same bird)
Rohan Duck [4] (D'Artagnan's proprietary Pekin-Moulard cross, printed by name on fine-dining menus as often as Moulard is; a guest reads it as a farm or a place, and it pairs with the Moulard card)

Pekin Duck [3] (Long Island Duck; the breed most American duck breast comes from and the confusable the guest brings up every time, Peking duck the dish versus Pekin the bird; the Duck Breast card teaches the cut, not the bird)
Elk [3] (elk loin and elk chop on mountain-state and steakhouse menus; the guest asks whether it is gamier than venison, and the deck holds no game mammal but venison and rabbit)
Wild Boar [3] (cinghiale on Italian menus, boar ragu and boar chop; the guest asks how it differs from pork; arguably a 2 by frequency, but the deck has no card for it under any term)

Frog Legs [3] (cuisses de grenouille at French bistros and Cajun menus; it belongs beside Escargot as the other thing a nervous guest needs a sentence about; rarer than escargot on American menus, so 3)
Pig's Ear [3] (crispy pig ear on gastropub and tapas menus, oreja; the guest asks whether it is actually the ear and what the texture is)
sections.note: Read the brief in full; none of its Lexicon candidates belong to Poultry, Game & Offal (all fruit, fungi, spice, vegetable and technique entries), so no proposal carries a lexiconSlug. Checked every proposal against everyCard terms and aliases in the brief: none is a card or a spelling variant (Chicken Oysters is a deliberate confusable with fish/Oysters, not a variant). Considered and set aside: Wild Boar and Frog Legs sit at Level 2 by the standard, beside Escargot; Veal is Level 1; Elk and Bison are animals that Venison's sentence largely covers; Veal Kidneys and Capon are honest Level 4 words but rarer on American menus than the four chosen; Foie Gras Torchon is a preparation and belongs to the preparations proposer; Gizzards are folded into the Duck Hearts card's mention. With four gains the section would hold 6 at Level III and 2 at Level IV.

proposals.reason: The prized heart of the pork leg, boned, bladder-wrapped and aged in the fog of Zibello; the most expensive thing on an Italian salumi board and the one a senior server must set beside Prosciutto (fd_0074) and Jamon Iberico (fd_0082), which the deck already teaches. Rare on menus, asked about whenever it appears, and it takes real explaining: by the standard that is Chef. It is also the section's second Level IV beside Lomo, which the roster asked for. No card or alias covers it; no Lexicon candidate holds it.
proposals.guestsAsk: How is this different from prosciutto, and why is it twice the price?
proposals.menuLine: Culatello di Zibello, 24 months, gnocco fritto, mostarda

proposals.reason: The Tuscan fennel-seed salami, printed by name on the salumi board of nearly every good Italian-leaning American restaurant and never called salami on the menu, so the server has to know it. The deck holds Soppressata and 'Nduja but no fennel salami and no Tuscan one. A specialist product needing a sentence beyond 'salami': Sous Chef. Unchallenged; stands.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is the flavor in this one, is it anise?
proposals.menuLine: Salumi: finocchiona, coppa, mortadella, pickled vegetables, grissini

proposals.reason: The charcuterie item guests ask about more than any other, because the name misleads: not cheese but the meat of the head set in its own gelatin, sliced cold. On house charcuterie boards at good American restaurants, on French menus as fromage de tete and Italian ones as coppa di testa (a different product from the Coppa card fd_0066, the neck muscle, which the card must say). Cooked charcuterie in the family of the section's Pate, Rillettes and Terrine. Needs a careful explanation and a steady face: Sous Chef. Unchallenged; stands.
proposals.guestsAsk: Wait, is head cheese actually cheese? What is in it?
proposals.menuLine: House charcuterie: head cheese, chicken liver mousse, duck rillettes, whole-grain mustard, cornichons

proposals.reason: Classical French blood sausage, cooked charcuterie beside the deck's Pate, Rillettes and Terrine, and a fixture on French bistro and fine-dining menus in America, usually with apple. The word hides what it is, so guests ask, and the answer (pork blood, fat, onion, spice, cooked, served hot) must be given plainly. Amended on the challenger's point: the card carries the aliases Blood Sausage, Black Pudding and Morcilla, because the gastropub prints blood sausage, the British-leaning menu black pudding and the Spanish board morcilla, and a card titled only Boudin Noir would teach none of them. The card's body must also say it is not the Cajun rice boudin. Fine-dining vocabulary: Sous Chef.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that really blood? What does it taste like?
proposals.menuLine: Boudin noir, caramelized apple, pommes puree, cider jus

dispositions.reason: No challenge was raised; the proposal stands unchanged at Level 4. It is the section's only new Chef-level word and the roster's first purpose.
No challenge was raised; the proposal stands unchanged at Level 3.
No challenge was raised; the proposal stands unchanged at Level 3, with the note that its body must set coppa di testa apart from the Coppa card.
Kept at Level 3, amended: the card now carries Blood Sausage, Black Pudding and Morcilla as aliases (the challenger's Morcilla point) and its body sets the Cajun rice boudin apart.

Real and on French bistro boards, but the guest's question ('is this like salami?') is answered in one sentence, yes, the French dry-cured salami, which is the Level II standard, not this roster's band; the deck's Soppressata and Charcuterie already give a server the concept. Also over the four-word cap against stronger words. Flag it for the Level II pass.

A compound the deck's own cards decode: Prosciutto (fd_0074) gives the cure and Duck Breast (fd_0056, Magret) the cut. Rather than a card, the Prosciutto card's body should carry one line that prosciutto-style cures of duck breast, lamb and beef appear on house boards, which answers 'is this really prosciutto?' without misleading anyone.

The most-asked tapas question is real, but serrano is the everyday Spanish white-pig ham, on a par with Prosciutto at Level 1 and explained in a sentence against Iberico: Level II by the standard, outside this roster's band. The Jamon Iberico card (fd_0082) should name serrano as its contrast in its body; flag the word itself for the Level II pass.

Rare on American menus even at Spanish restaurants, and the word is a confusable in its own right: on Mexican menus cecina is thin salted fresh beef, not the air-dried cecina de Leon, so a card would have to teach two products from two countries for a word few servers will print. Prefer words that appear on menus. The Bresaola card (fd_0079) can name cecina de Leon as its Spanish cousin.

The strongest of the rejected and the first to add if the cap lifts: the soft Mallorcan paprika sausage is the confusable partner of 'Nduja and now appears as sobrasada toast with honey. But it is on Spanish-leaning menus only, and the four kept words are each on more American menus and asked about more often; the section takes four. The 'Nduja card (fd_0081) should name sobrasada as its contrast.

Regional: it appears on Cajun and Southern menus, and the owner removed the Southern section from this deck; Andouille and Tasso survived because they travel onto general American menus, and rice boudin has not to the same degree. The Boudin Noir card's body sets the two apart, which meets the challenger's stated need without a card.
Added as an alias on Boudin Noir with Blood Sausage and Black Pudding, so the card teaches the word on the Spanish board, the gastropub and the French bistro alike.

A true gap, but at Level 2 it lies outside this roster's Level III and IV band, so it does not join this list; the flag stands and is carried to the Level II pass, where it belongs beside Coppa and Soppressata.

Not a card for this band: the Italian header word for the board belongs as an alias on the Charcuterie card (fd_0078), which is an edit to an existing Level 1 card, not a Level III or IV proposal. Carried as a recommendation to the alias pass.

missing: Saucisson Sec [3] — the French dry salami on every French bistro board in America (Balthazar, Frenchette, Le Pichet houses print it by name); the deck holds Italian and Calabrian salami and no French one; guests ask 'is this like salami?'

Duck Prosciutto [3] — the house-cured duck breast on nearly every American house charcuterie board; not pork and not leg, so the Prosciutto card (fd_0074) misleads a server who has only that; guests ask 'is this really prosciutto?'

Jamón Serrano [3] — the everyday Spanish ham beside Jamón Ibérico (fd_0082); the single most-asked question at a tapas table is 'what is the difference between serrano and ibérico?', and the Ibérico card is not an alias for it
Cecina [4] — Spanish air-dried beef (menus print 'cecina de León'), the Spanish foil to Bresaola (fd_0079) on Spanish and tapas menus; rare, asked about, and a Level IV the section badly needs
Sobrasada [4] — Mallorcan soft paprika sausage, now on Spanish-leaning menus as sobrasada toast with honey; the confusable partner of 'Nduja (fd_0081) and nowhere in the deck

Boudin (Cajun) [3] — the proposer named it and then left it out; pork, rice and liver in casing, on Cajun and Southern menus as links or boudin balls, and the section already carries Andouille and Tasso; the Boudin Noir card must set the two apart

Morcilla — not a new card but a required alias on Boudin Noir with Blood Sausage and Black Pudding; the Spanish board prints morcilla and the gastropub prints blood sausage, and a card titled only Boudin Noir teaches neither
Mortadella [2] — outside this roster's band, but the proposer's own Finocchiona menu line prints it and the deck has no card under any term; flag it for the Level II pass
Salumi [1] — outside the band; the Italian header word for the board, on more American menus than 'charcuterie', and the Charcuterie card (fd_0078) should carry it as an alias
sections.note: All four are absent from everyCard under any term or alias, and none of the brief's Lexicon candidates covers cured meat, so no lexiconSlug applies. Considered and left out: Mortadella and Jamon Serrano (both common enough to be Level 2 by the standard, confusable pairs with Coppa/Pancetta and Jamon Iberico; worth adding, but not at III or IV), Duck Prosciutto (frequent on American boards at Level 3, but a reviewer may read it as a variant of the Prosciutto card, so it is second choice behind Boudin Noir), Saucisson Sec (a French salami; explains in half a sentence, so honestly Level 2), Cotechino and Sobrasada (Level 4 candidates but genuinely rare on American menus). One gap to flag outside this roster's scope: the deck has no Salami card at all, which by the standard is a Level 1 word.

proposals.reason: A chuck steak from the serratus ventralis under the shoulder blade, named and marketed in the last twenty years and now a fixture on steakhouse and wine-bar menus as the marbled, well-priced grilling steak. The deck's Shoulder card teaches chuck as a braising cut and Flat Iron as the one tender chuck steak; the Denver is the other one, a different muscle, and a server has to say it is a true steak (grilled medium-rare, sliced across the grain) and not a braise. Specialist cut, on menus, needs a sentence: Level III on the Coulotte pattern. Aliases: Zabuton (the same muscle as wagyu and omakase steakhouses print it, A5 Zabuton), Underblade Steak.
proposals.guestsAsk: What part of the cow is a Denver steak, and is it tender like a ribeye?
proposals.menuLine: Denver Steak, 10 oz, charred scallion, bone marrow butter, hand-cut fries  46

proposals.reason: The small shoulder muscle that is the second most tender on the animal after the tenderloin, roasted whole and sliced like a small filet, and printed under its anatomical name or as Petite Tender, Shoulder Tender or Bistro Filet. It has been the value steak at gastropubs, wine bars and farm-to-table rooms for a decade, so it is not rare, and the explanation is one sentence (a chuck muscle that eats like filet at a third of the price), with no classical technique or provenance behind it: that is Level III with Coulotte and Bavette, not Level IV with Bottarga and Ballotine. Nothing in the deck names it; Flat Iron is the other tender chuck cut and a different muscle. Aliases: Petite Tender, Shoulder Tender, Bistro Filet, so the server recognises it under whichever name the house prints.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is teres major, is that beef, and why is it so much cheaper than the filet?
proposals.menuLine: Teres Major, roasted whole and sliced, celery root purée, black garlic jus, watercress  42

proposals.reason: The thick center-cut tenderloin roast for two, on steakhouse and fine-dining menus with béarnaise and usually carved tableside. The Tenderloin card teaches the muscle and aliases Filet Mignon, Beef Filet and Fillet, but not this word, and the guest asks about it as a word: whether it is a filet, how one roast is cooked for two people, and why it is priced whole. A classical French word that needs a sentence about the center cut, the carving and the sauce: Level III. It takes the slot Tri-Tip held because it is fine-dining vocabulary and Tri-Tip is not.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is chateaubriand a filet mignon, and how does it work for two if we want it cooked differently?
proposals.menuLine: Chateaubriand for Two, center-cut tenderloin, carved tableside, béarnaise, pommes soufflées  148

proposals.reason: The thin, heavily marbled fan of Ibérico pork from behind the shoulder, hidden against the belly fat (hence 'secret'), now a fixture on Spanish and tapas menus in American cities and on fine-dining menus that buy whole Ibérico pigs. American menus print the two words together: the Ibérico is the selling point and the reason for the price, and the guest reads and asks about both. It is seared hot and served pink, which alarms guests who expect pork cooked through, so the server explains the cut, the breed and why it is served that way. The deck teaches Jamón Ibérico as a cured ham; this is the fresh cut, and Pork Belly and Shoulder do not cover it. Rare, specialist, deeply explained: Level IV. Alias: Secreto. The card's body should name its two siblings on the same menus, Presa (the shoulder end) and Pluma (the feather at the tip of the loin), since the server who can explain secreto is asked about those in the same breath.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is secreto Ibérico, and is it safe that the pork comes pink in the middle?
proposals.menuLine: Secreto Ibérico, grilled over coals, romesco, charred spring onions, Maldon salt  48

dispositions.reason: Moved to Level III. By the standard's own signals it sits with Coulotte and Bavette: on gastropub and wine-bar menus for a decade as the value steak, explained in one sentence, no classical technique behind it. Level IV in this deck is Bottarga, Ballotine, Acquerello, which are rare and deep; Teres Major is neither. Petite Tender, Shoulder Tender and Bistro Filet added as aliases.

Renamed Secreto Ibérico with Secreto kept as an alias. American menus almost never print the bare word; the breed is the selling point and the guest asks about the two words together. Level IV stands.

Added at Level III. On steakhouse and fine-dining menus as the tenderloin roast for two, carved tableside; the Tenderloin card's aliases do not include it and the guest asks about it as a word (is it a filet, how is it cooked for two, why priced whole). Classical, needs a sentence, fine-dining vocabulary. It takes the slot Tri-Tip held; see that disposition.

Dropped from this roster. The roster takes Level III and IV words, and by the standard Tri-Tip is Level II: common at good restaurants (a Santa Maria and West Coast standby that many American guests know on day one), explained in a sentence, and not fine-dining vocabulary the way Coulotte and Bavette are. It is a good card for a Level II pass, not this one, and Chateaubriand outranks it on fine-dining menus.

Does not earn one of four slots. American menus, including most fine-dining rooms, print Lamb Loin for this cut; Saddle appears at a handful of classical French rooms and in cookery books, and the brief prefers menu words over book words. Rack of Lamb is a different cut, so the deck does not teach it, but its menu frequency is below every word kept.

A fair Level III word (the fresh coppa muscle, grilled and sliced pink, that the cured Coppa card does not cover) but the roster is capped at four and it ranks below Chateaubriand, Denver Steak and Teres Major on how often a server meets it and is asked. The strongest of the rejected words; it should lead the next Meat Cuts pass if the section reopens.

Not separate cards. They are different cuts, so they cannot be aliases of Secreto Ibérico, and two more Level IV Ibérico cards would spend three of four slots on one pig. The Secreto Ibérico card's body names both as the siblings printed on the same menus (presa the shoulder end, pluma the feather at the loin tip), which is where the server meets them and how the question arrives.

At most Level II: a plain English cut common on Southern and modern American menus, explained in a sentence, and the guest's question (what part is it) is answered by the face the deck already teaches through Cheek (aliases Pork Cheek) and Guanciale (the cured jowl). Outside this roster's levels and not a gap that costs a slot.

A plain English word that needs no vocabulary; the guest's question is reassurance (is it really the neck) not definition, and the Shank and Short Rib cards already teach why a hard-working cut is braised until it yields. Level II if it were carded at all, so outside this roster.

Accepted as an alias, not a card: it is the bone-in rib for two, the same cut the Ribeye card (fd_0090) already teaches under Cowboy Steak and Tomahawk. Add Côte de Boeuf to that card's aliases so the server recognises it under the French name a bistro or fine-dining menu prints.
Added as an alias on the Denver Steak card. Same serratus ventralis muscle, printed as A5 Zabuton on wagyu and omakase steakhouse menus; one card, two names.

challenges.because: It is a specialist cut on exactly the Coulotte and Bavette pattern, which the standard itself files at Level III: on menus at gastropubs, wine bars and farm-to-table rooms for a decade as the value steak, explained in one sentence (a shoulder muscle that eats like filet), with no classical technique or provenance behind it. Level IV in this deck is Acquerello, Bottarga, Ballotine: rare and deep. Teres Major is neither rare nor deep; it is Level III with Petite Tender, Shoulder Tender and Bistro Filet as aliases so the server recognises it under whichever name the house prints.

American menus almost never print the bare word: the Ibérico is the selling point and the reason for the price, and the guest reads and asks about the two words together. Keep Secreto as an alias. Level IV stands: rare, specialist, needs both the anatomy and the served-pink explanation.

missing: Chateaubriand [3]: the thick center-cut tenderloin roast for two on steakhouse and fine-dining menus, carved tableside, béarnaise; the Tenderloin card aliases Filet Mignon, Beef Filet and Fillet but not this, and the guest asks whether it is a filet, how it is cooked for two and why it is priced whole; a classical word that needs a sentence, Level III

Saddle of Lamb [3]: fine-dining menus print Saddle or Lamb Saddle for the whole loin section roasted on the bone, and guests ask what a saddle is; Rack of Lamb (Level 1) is a different cut and nothing else in the deck names it

Pork Collar [3]: the fresh coppa muscle, on modern American menus as Ibérico or Berkshire pork collar, grilled and sliced pink; the Coppa card in cured teaches the cured muscle, not the fresh cut a guest asks about

Presa [4] and Pluma [4]: the other two fresh Ibérico cuts that share every menu Secreto appears on (the shoulder end and the feather at the tip of the loin); a server who can explain secreto is asked about these in the same breath, and the proposer named one of the three
Pork Jowl [3]: fresh jowl, crisped or braised, on Southern and modern American menus; the Guanciale card teaches the cured jowl, not the cut, and the guest asks what part it is
Lamb Neck [3]: braised lamb neck is now a fixture on good American menus and guests ask whether that is really the neck; Shoulder and Shank (Level 1) do not cover it

Côte de Boeuf [3]: the French bone-in rib for two on bistro and fine-dining menus; if the reconciler counts it as taught by the Ribeye card (Cowboy, Tomahawk) then add it there as an alias, because the guest asks about it under this name
Zabuton: same muscle as the proposed Denver Steak, printed on wagyu and omakase steakhouse menus as A5 Zabuton; belongs on the Denver Steak card as an alias, not as a separate card
sections.note: Four proposals, two at Level III and two at Level IV, none carried by any deck term or alias and none a spelling variant (the everyCard list holds Coulotte/Picanha and Bavette/Sirloin Flap as the only bottom-sirloin cards, Shoulder/Chuck and Flat Iron/Top Blade as the only chuck cards, Jamón Ibérico only as a cured ham). No Lexicon candidate in the brief is a meat cut, so no slugs. Held back on purpose: Chateaubriand (common on steakhouse menus as 'for two', but it is the center of the Tenderloin the deck already teaches, so a reviewer could call it covered); Lamb Saddle and Lamb Neck (fine-dining but far less asked about than the four above); Osso Buco (a preparation of the Shank card, belongs to preparations if anywhere); Côte de Boeuf and Prime Rib (bone-in ribeye and rib roast, covered in spirit by the Ribeye card); Pork Collar (fresh coppa, too close to the Coppa card in cured). Observed, not proposed because it is Level I: the deck has no Sirloin / Top Sirloin card, which is an everyday steakhouse word.

proposals.reason: Sea urchin roe (the gonad, not a true roe, not a fish, not shellfish meat) is on the raw-bar, crudo and pasta sections of most fine-dining American menus and many good ones, sold by origin (Santa Barbara, Hokkaido, Maine). It takes more than a sentence to explain and the deck's Roe and Caviar cards do not cover it; no card or alias in everyCard names uni, sea urchin or urchin. Fine-dining vocabulary with a specialist product behind it: Level III, beside Crudo and Turbot. Stands unchallenged.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is uni, is it a fish? Is that the orange stuff, and what does it taste like?
proposals.menuLine: Bucatini, Santa Barbara uni, Calabrian chile, lemon, toasted breadcrumbs 34

proposals.reason: The classical fine-dining flatfish, flown in from the North Sea and Channel, cooked whole and filleted tableside, nearly always at market price and usually the most expensive fish on the page. A server must explain the price, that it is a true sole (not the flounder or fluke that American menus print as sole) and the tableside service. The deck holds Flounder and Halibut at Level I and Turbot at III but nothing at this end of the flatfish case; no sole of any kind appears in everyCard. Classical and specialist: Level III beside Turbot and Meunière. Stands unchallenged.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is it really from Dover? Why is it market price, and how is it different from the flounder?
proposals.menuLine: Dover Sole Meunière, filleted tableside, brown butter, capers, lemon MP

proposals.reason: The Norway lobster (Dublin Bay prawn; scampi in Italian), a slender clawed crustacean between shrimp and lobster, flown in live or frozen at sea and sold at the top of the fine-dining page, roasted, butter-poached or raw as a tail. Two confusions to untangle: scampi is a preparation in America and this animal in Italy, and a prawn is a shrimp but this is not. The deck's Shrimp/Prawns, Lobster and Crawfish cards do not cover it. Moved from IV to III on the challenge: it is the shellfish twin of Turbot, an imported European specialist product explained in a sentence, and it appears on tasting menus at least as often as turbot does; Level IV is for the rarer or deeper word (Bottarga, Ballotine).
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that a shrimp or a baby lobster? Is it the same thing as scampi?
proposals.menuLine: Roasted Langoustines, brown butter, tarragon, fennel pollen, sea salt 48

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list and placed at IV, not the III proposed. Escolar is on upscale seafood and steakhouse menus under its own name and on sushi and raw menus as White Tuna, Super White Tuna or Walu; guests ask what it is. It is a snake mackerel, not a tuna, and its wax-ester oil means a large portion has digestive consequences for many guests, so the house serves it in small portions and a server must be able to say so without alarming the table. That is the floor-safety knowledge a senior server must own, which is the Level IV standard; the deck's Tuna card is Level I with no alias and nothing in everyCard carries escolar, white tuna or walu. The section had one Level IV card (Bottarga); this gives it a second that a server actually meets on a menu.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is escolar? Is it the same as the white tuna at the sushi place, and why is the portion small?
proposals.menuLine: Grilled Escolar, charred leeks, Meyer lemon beurre blanc, salsa verde 42

dispositions.reason: The challenger is right on the level: hamachi crudo and hamachi collar are on the raw section of good restaurants everywhere, the yellowtail/yellowfin mix-up is a one-sentence confusable pair, and it is more common on American menus than the section's existing Level III fish (Cobia, Tilefish, Wreckfish). By the standard that is Level II beside Branzino. This roster places only Level III and IV words, so Hamachi is dropped from it rather than kept at 3. It remains a real gap (no Yellowtail or Amberjack anywhere in everyCard) and should be written as a Level II fish card in a Level II pass.

Moved from IV to III. Turbot at III is the parallel: an imported European specialist product at the top of the fine-dining page, explained in one sentence, and on tasting menus at least as often as turbot. The scampi and prawn confusions are a sentence each, not senior-server-only knowledge. Level IV is for the rarer or deeply classical word (Bottarga, Ballotine, Acquerello). Kept in the list at 3.

A real menu word, but it sits where Branzino sits: the other whole-roasted Mediterranean fish, common at good restaurants, explained in one sentence, and the guest's question ('is it the same as branzino?') is the definition of a Level II confusable pair. Madai is a different species (Pagrus major) that a card conflating it with Sparus aurata would get wrong. It belongs at Level II beside Branzino, not in this III/IV roster, and the section is at its four.

A fine-dining raw-bar item, but a one-sentence variant of a Level I card (a long thin clam, sweet, served raw or flash-grilled), on fewer menus and asked about less than the four words the section takes. It could ride as an alias on the Clams card or wait for a slot; it does not displace Uni, Dover Sole, Langoustine or Escolar.

A legitimate Level III word, but the classical-European-market-price slot is already held twice in this section, by Turbot (existing, III) and Dover Sole (this roster), and John Dory is rarer on American menus than either. A third such fish is a word from the book more than from the menu, and the roster prefers the menu. Revisit if a later pass wants a fifth fine-dining fish.

A strong menu word and a genuine gap, but it is a one-sentence cut of a Level I fish ('the fatty belly of the bluefin, graded otoro and chutoro'), on nearly every good sushi-inflected menu, which by frequency and length of explanation is Level II, not III. With the section at four it does not displace the four chosen. Recommend a line on the Tuna card, or a Level II card in a Level II pass.

The deck holds no Squid or Calamari card at all, and calamari is on nearly every American menu, a Level I gap. Teaching cuttlefish (seppia) before calamari is backwards: the guest's question is 'is it squid?', which needs the squid card to answer. Flag Calamari as a Level I gap for the fish section; cuttlefish can follow it later.

A brand name for New Zealand farmed king (chinook) salmon, printed on menus as a brand the way Acquerello is, but the guest's question is answered in half a sentence ('a branded farmed king salmon from New Zealand, richer than the Atlantic you know'), and a card on a brand is thin next to the four chosen. Better carried as a line on the Salmon card.

A real West Coast fine-dining product, live, head-on, roe-bearing, seasonal and at market price, but regional, and a one-sentence variant of Shrimp/Prawns. With the section at four it does not displace Langoustine, which carries the harder shellfish confusions. A fair alias or later Level III card for a West Coast house.

Added, and placed at Level IV rather than the III the challenger gave it. The word is on menus (as Escolar, White Tuna, Super White Tuna, Walu) and guests ask what it is, but what makes it a card is the duty: a senior server must know it is not a tuna and that a large portion has consequences, and must say so tactfully. That is knowledge a senior server must own, the Level IV standard, and the section had only Bottarga at IV.

A fair Level IV word but rare on American menus outside Pacific Northwest raw bars and top sushi counters; the roster prefers words a server meets on a menu over words in the book, and the section's Level IV slot goes to Escolar, which is met far more often and carries a safety duty.

A legitimate Level IV shellfish (rare, expensive, sold by piece, mostly farmed Monterey abalone on West Coast fine-dining and tasting menus) and the confusion with the deck's Abalone Mushroom card is a real hook. It loses the section's fourth slot to Escolar on menu frequency and the safety duty. Recommend a line on the Abalone Mushroom card ('named for the shellfish, not the shellfish') and a card of its own if a later pass widens the section.

Kampachi (Hiramasa, Kona Kampachi) is explained entirely in terms of hamachi ('the farmed Hawaiian amberjack, a cousin of hamachi, leaner'), and the guest's question is 'is it hamachi?'. Hamachi was ruled a Level II word this roster cannot place, so kampachi has no card to lean on yet. Revisit at Level IV once Hamachi is written at II.

challenges.because: Right word, wrong level. By the standard, Level II is 'common at a good restaurant, needs a sentence to explain, the main confusable pairs' (Branzino is its example), and hamachi is exactly that: hamachi crudo and hamachi collar are on the raw section of good restaurants everywhere, not only fine dining, and the yellowtail/yellowfin mix-up is a one-sentence confusable pair a Level II server untangles weekly. It is more common on American menus than the section's existing Level III fish (Cobia, Tilefish, Wreckfish). The deck teaches nothing like it (no Yellowtail or Amberjack anywhere in everyCard), so it belongs in the deck, at 2.

Level IV is for the rare or deeply classical word (Bottarga, Acquerello, Banyuls). Langoustine is the shellfish twin of Turbot, which the section already places at III: an imported European specialist product sold at the top of the fine-dining page and explained in one sentence ('a small clawed cousin of the lobster, sweeter, the thing Italians mean by scampi'). It appears on tasting menus in any fine-dining town at least as often as turbot does, and the scampi question is a sentence, not senior-server-only knowledge. Not taught under any term or alias (Shrimp/Prawns, Lobster and Crawfish do not cover it), so keep it, beside Turbot at 3.

missing: Dorade (printed also as Orata, Daurade, Sea Bream; Madai on Japanese-leaning menus) [3]: the other whole-roasted Mediterranean fish, on fine-dining menus beside or instead of branzino, and the question is always 'is it the same as branzino?'; the Branzino card's aliases do not include it.
Razor Clams [3]: fine-dining raw-bar and crudo word; guests ask what it is and how it is eaten; the Clams card's aliases (Littlenecks, Quahogs, Steamers) do not cover it.
John Dory [3]: the classical European fine-dining fish (Saint-Pierre) sold at market price beside Dover sole and turbot; guests ask what it is and why the price.

Toro (Otoro, Chutoro) [3]: bluefin belly on fine-dining raw sections and every good sushi-inflected American menu; guests ask what toro is and why it costs three times the tuna; the Tuna card is Level I and has no such alias.

Cuttlefish (Seppia on Italian menus) [3]: on fine-dining Italian and Spanish-leaning menus, confused with squid; the deck holds no Squid or Calamari card, and cuttlefish is the one a guest asks about.

Ora King (printed as Ora King Salmon) [3]: the branded New Zealand king salmon named on menus by brand, the way Acquerello names a rice; guests ask what 'Ora King' means and why it is not the salmon they know; the Salmon card does not carry it.

Spot Prawns [3]: the West Coast live, head-on, roe-bearing prawn served raw or barely cooked at fine dining, seasonal and at market price; the Shrimp card's Prawns alias is the generic word, not this product.
Escolar (printed as White Tuna or Walu on menus) [3]: the floor-safety word; a server must know that 'white tuna' is not a tuna and that a large portion has consequences, and guests ask what it is.
Geoduck [4]: rare Pacific Northwest clam served raw at top raw bars and sushi counters; guests cannot pronounce it and ask what it is.
Abalone [4]: rare, expensive, fine-dining shellfish, sold by piece; the deck holds Abalone Mushroom (named for it) but not the animal, and guests ask which one they are getting.
Kampachi (also Hiramasa; printed as Kona Kampachi) [4]: the farmed Hawaiian amberjack on fine-dining crudo sections, confused with hamachi, which is the question guests ask; senior-server word.
sections.note: Brief read in full (2,696 lines); the everyCard list and every alias were searched for each proposal and its confusables (Sea Urchin, Sole, Yellowtail, Amberjack, Scampi, Norway Lobster, Dublin Bay Prawn) and none is taught. The Lexicon candidates list holds no fish entry, so no lexiconSlug is given. Runners-up the section could still take if a fifth were wanted: Sablefish / Black Cod (Level III, the miso black cod confusion: not a cod), Geoduck (Level IV, pronunciation and what it is), and Osetra / Kaluga as caviar grades (Level IV) though that one borders the existing Caviar card. Left out as below Level III: Octopus, Dungeness, King Crab, Stone Crab, Mackerel; left out as already covered by an alias: Razor Clams and Bay Scallops (under Clams and Scallops), Spot Prawns (under Shrimp/Prawns), Ikura and trout roe (under Roe).

proposals.reason: The Alba white truffle (Tuber magnatum) is the rarest thing a server carries to a table: a six-to-eight-week autumn season, priced by the gram at market, never cooked, shaved raw over eggs, pasta or risotto at the table. The Level I Truffle card (fd_0147) says 'white shaved raw' in half a sentence; it does not carry the season, the market price, why the kitchen will not heat it, or why no half-portion is offered, and a senior server is asked all four every October. Rare, expensive and deeply specialist: Level IV, beside Acquerello and Bottarga, which it is often shaved over. Unchallenged; stands.
proposals.guestsAsk: Why is white truffle so much more than black, and why can't you cook it into the dish?
proposals.menuLine: Risotto Acquerello, brown butter, Alba white truffle shaved tableside (MP)

proposals.reason: The Japanese pine mushroom reaches good American tasting menus every autumn, priced like truffle and served in a way a server must describe: barely cooked, torn into a dobin mushi broth or over rice, with sudachi. Guests do not recognise the name, cannot picture it, and are surprised by the pine-and-cinnamon spice; the American harvest is a Pacific Northwest relative of the Japanese fungus, which the senior server should know. Rare, seasonal and never farmed: Level IV by the standard, where the Lexicon also holds it. Unchallenged; stands.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is matsutake and why is a mushroom priced like truffle?
proposals.menuLine: Matsutake dobin mushi, dashi, sudachi, ginkgo nut

proposals.reason: Menus print 'summer truffle' (Tuber aestivum) from May to September, and 'Burgundy truffle' for the same species' autumn crop, at a quarter to half the winter supplement; it is the truffle behind most warm-weather truffle dishes and the one the Truffle card (fd_0147) does not settle, since that card teaches the black-versus-white split and neither name. The floor question is the imposter question: why this truffle is cheaper and why it barely smells, the honest answer being that its aroma is a fraction of the Perigord's and it is there for the look and the texture. Fine-dining vocabulary that needs a sentence and a half: Level III beside Black Trumpet. Added on the challenger's list in place of the dropped Black Truffle; the Lexicon has no entry for it.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is this the same as a real truffle, and why is it so much cheaper than the one you had in winter?
proposals.menuLine: Burrata, summer truffle, wildflower honey, grilled sourdough (supplement 14)

proposals.reason: A wild autumn-to-winter mushroom that New American, Cal-Italian and farm-to-table kitchens roast whole alongside chanterelles, and the one wild mushroom whose name stops a guest cold. Its identifier is the soft spines under the cap in place of gills (hence 'sweet tooth'), it eats like a firmer chanterelle, and the server needs a sentence to reassure the table. Foraged, never farmed, and rarer on menus than the Level II Chanterelle, it sits at Level III beside Black Trumpet, the section's one existing Level III card. The Lexicon holds it as hedgehog-mushroom at its Level II, so the writer has material; it is not among the brief's Level III/IV candidates, so no slug is claimed here. Unchallenged; stands.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is that an actual hedgehog, and what does it taste like?
proposals.menuLine: Roasted hedgehog mushrooms, sunchoke, sherry, thyme, toasted sourdough

dispositions.reason: Dropped. I read fd_0147 in tools/derive/floor-deck/mushrooms.mjs: its line is 'Tagliatelle, butter, shaved black truffle', its origin is 'Black winter truffles from France, white from Piedmont in Italy', and its why-text already gives 'white shaved raw, black often warmed gently in fat'. The deck therefore teaches black truffle under the term Truffle, and what the proposal adds (season, supplement) is a paragraph on that card, not a new word. Four truffle cards in a 16-card section is too many. The Lexicon candidate black-truffle stays uncarded, which is what a Level I umbrella card implies. The freed truffle slot goes to Summer Truffle, the one truffle question fd_0147 does not settle.

Added at Level III. Not taught under any term or alias: fd_0147 names neither 'summer' nor 'Burgundy' truffle and its split is black-versus-white, not winter-versus-summer. It is a menu word (May to September on most fine-dining menus that run a truffle supplement), the guest asks why it is cheaper and why it barely smells, and it belongs squarely to 'what a truffle is and is not'. Level III by the standard: fine-dining vocabulary needing a sentence and a half, not the rare specialist word of Level IV.

Does not belong to this section. Corn smut is a fungus but not a mushroom or a truffle, and it is cooked as a vegetable filling; the blurb holds 'cultivated and wild mushrooms' and truffles. It appears on Mexican menus at Mexican restaurants, not on the menu of the good or fine-dining American restaurant the deck is written for, and with the section at its four the roster allows, a fifth card that would sit here only by the question 'is it a mushroom' is not the best use of a slot. If the deck ever gains a Mexican pantry section, it goes there at Level IV.

A real menu word and the strongest of the five rejected, but the section is at the four the roster allows, and it ranks below the four kept: rarer on menus nationally than summer truffle, seen mostly on Pacific Northwest and New England menus in late summer, and its whole floor answer is one line ('no shellfish; the name is for the red-orange color of a mold that grows over a wild mushroom'). That line belongs as a note or a notThis on a mushroom card, and it is the first word to add if this section is ever allowed a fifth at Level III.

A West Coast dessert-menu curiosity, on a handful of menus for a few weeks a year, rarer than any card the section holds including Abalone Mushroom. The guest's disbelief that a mushroom is in the dessert is charming but the word fails the standard's first signal, how often it is on menus; it is a book word more than a menu word, and the roster says to prefer the menu.

The winter chanterelle is a small cousin of the Level II Chanterelle (fd_0141), and the guest's one question, 'is it a chanterelle and why is it smaller and cheaper', is answered by that card in a sentence: a smaller, thinner winter cousin, hollow-stemmed, cheaper because it is more plentiful. A card would repeat fd_0141. It is a distinct species, so not an alias; the right home is a line on the Chanterelle card's notThis, not a new Level IV word, and it is regional (West Coast, November to February).

A cultivated mushroom that appears on menus as one name inside a 'roasted mushrooms' list, almost never as the dish. The floor answer is one sentence: a small brown-capped Italian mushroom in clumps, firm and nutty. By the standard that is a Level II word at most, and the roster asks for Level III and IV; the section's Beech Mushroom (fd_0139) already teaches the clumped brown-cap confusable a guest cannot place.

challenges.because: Already taught by fd_0147 Truffle (Level I). That card's own menu line is 'Tagliatelle, butter, shaved black truffle', its origin field reads 'Black winter truffles from France, white from Piedmont in Italy', and its why-text already gives the split the proposer claims is missing: 'white shaved raw, black often warmed gently in fat'. What is left for a Level III card (the season, the supplement) is a paragraph on the Truffle card, not a new word; and a 16-card section carrying Truffle, Truffle Oil, Black Truffle and White Truffle is four truffle cards. The floor question at Level III is not black versus white, which the Level I card answers, but the imposter: see Summer Truffle in the missing list.

missing: Summer Truffle [3] (menus print 'summer truffle' or 'Burgundy truffle' May to September at half the supplement; the guest asks why this truffle is cheaper and why it barely smells; the winter-versus-summer imposter is the one truffle question fd_0147 does not settle)
Huitlacoche [4] (corn smut, on every serious Mexican menu in quesadillas, tamales and sauces; guests ask 'what is huitlacoche' and then 'is it a mushroom'; nothing in the deck touches it)

Lobster Mushroom [3] (summer-to-fall wild mushroom on Pacific Northwest and New England menus; the guest's first question is a shellfish-allergy question, 'is there lobster in it', which makes it a floor word, and fd_0136 Lobster is the shellfish, not this)
Candy Cap [4] (the maple-scented mushroom that lands on West Coast dessert menus as candy cap ice cream, panna cotta or creme brulee; guests do not believe a mushroom is in their dessert and ask)

Yellowfoot [4] (winter chanterelle, printed 'yellowfoot' or 'yellow foot chanterelle' on West Coast menus November to February; guests ask whether it is a chanterelle and why it is smaller and cheaper; fd_0141's aliases do not carry it)

Pioppino [3] (printed 'pioppino' or 'pioppini' in the roasted-mushroom plates of farm-to-table and Cal-Italian menus; a clumped brown-capped mushroom guests cannot place and ask about; Beech Mushroom fd_0139 is the confusable, not the same word)
sections.note: Four proposed, the cap. Three carry Lexicon entries (black-truffle, white-truffle, matsutake); Hedgehog Mushroom does not. If the reconciler rules that the Level I Truffle card already covers the black-versus-white distinction, Matsutake and Hedgehog stand alone and the section would still gain one at each level. Considered and left out as thinner on American menus: Huitlacoche (Level IV, but only on upscale Mexican menus), Lobster Mushroom and Yellowfoot (regional and rarely printed), Summer or Burgundy Truffle (better taught inside the Black Truffle card as the cheaper imposter guests are sold), Candy Cap (dessert kitchens only), Pioppino and Nameko (farmed, seldom named on a menu). No existing term or alias in everyCard overlaps any proposal; Black Chanterelle (an alias of Black Trumpet) is a different mushroom from Black Truffle.

proposals.reason: The cream-soaked shreds that fill a burrata, now sold on their own as a spoonable cheese on tomato plates, pizzas and crostini at good and fine-dining restaurants. Not taught under any card or alias: the Burrata gist describes the filling but never names it. It takes a sentence to explain and a second sentence to disambiguate from the Roman egg-drop soup and the chocolate-chip gelato of the same name, which is the Sous Chef tier: fine-dining vocabulary, a specialist product, a confusable name. Unchallenged; stands as proposed.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is stracciatella the soup or the gelato? What is it doing on a tomato salad?
proposals.menuLine: Heirloom Tomatoes, stracciatella, basil oil, sourdough crumb

proposals.reason: The style word on a cheese course for a bloomy soft cheese enriched with added cream to at least 75 percent butterfat (Brillat-Savarin, Delice de Bourgogne, Saint-Andre, Mt Tam, Kunik), the cheese a fine-dining cart leads with. The deck teaches Bloomy Rind and Washed Rind as style words but has no card for this third style word a server must read off a cheese list. Renamed from the hyphenated French form on the challenger's point: American cheese lists print it as two words, triple creme, or in English as triple cream, so the card should carry Triple Cream as its alias. Sous Chef: a cheese-course term the guest asks about, explained in one sentence about cream and richness.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does triple crème mean? Is it like Brie, and is it strong?
proposals.menuLine: Cheese Course: Brillat-Savarin (triple crème, cow, Burgundy), quince paste, walnut bread

proposals.reason: The washed-rind cheese American menus actually print: on pizza bianca, folded into polenta and risotto, in a bistro grilled cheese, and on the cheese course, where guests ask about it because they fear the smell and are surprised to find it mild. Not taught under any term or alias; Washed Rind teaches the style at Level 4 with no named example, so the guided reader should meet the cheese at Sous Chef before the style at Chef, the way Bloomy Rind sits under Brebis. A specialist product with a one-sentence answer: a square cow's milk cheese from Lombardy, pungent orange rind, soft, sweet, fruity paste far gentler than its aroma. Added on the challenger's missing list, ahead of Clothbound and Alpine-Style, because it is on savory menus every service and not only on the cheese course.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is taleggio? Is it as strong as it smells?
proposals.menuLine: Soft Polenta, taleggio, roasted hen of the woods, thyme

proposals.reason: A soft, tangy northern Italian cheese, in the American kitchen almost always a mixed-milk Robiola Bosina or a fresh Robiola di Roccaverano of goat, used as a filling for stuffed pasta and as the cheese on the white pizza at fine-dining Italian houses. Rare enough that most servers have never tasted it and specialist enough that a Chef-level card is the right home, beside Brebis and Washed Rind: the guest wants the milk, the strength and whether a soft-cheese avoider can eat it. Unchallenged; stands as proposed, and it is this section's one Level IV gain.
proposals.guestsAsk: What kind of cheese is robiola? Is it goat, and is it strong?
proposals.menuLine: Agnolotti of robiola, brown butter, sage, toasted hazelnut

dispositions.reason: The challenger is right by the standard's own signals. It is on the menu at nearly every ambitious American restaurant, it is asked about at the first bread drop, and it takes exactly the one sentence the deck already gives Creme Fraiche at Level 2 and Buttermilk at Level 1 (cream ripened with live cultures before churning, so it tastes tangy). That is Chef de Partie, beside Creme Fraiche; the roster's aim of gaining Level III words does not make it a Level III word. Moved to Level 2, which puts it outside this roster, so it is dropped from the final list and should be handed to a Level II pass rather than lost: the deck still has no card for it.

Renamed to Triple Crème. American cheese lists and carts print it as two words, or in English as triple cream (Mt Tam, Kunik, Brillat-Savarin are all sold that way); the hyphen belongs to French cheese writing, not to menus. Triple Cream should be the card's alias so the English printing matches too. The word and its Level 3 stand: it is the third style word a server reads off a cheese course next to Bloomy Rind and Washed Rind, and no card or alias teaches it.

Added at Level 3, the fourth and last slot. It is the one washed-rind cheese a server at a good or fine-dining American restaurant sells by name, on savory plates every service and not only on the cheese course, and Washed Rind at Level 4 teaches the style with no named cheese under it. Of the challenger's seven, it is the one with the strongest menu presence and the most frequent guest question, so it takes the slot ahead of Clothbound and Alpine-Style.

A label claim, not a cheese word: the deck files its siblings Grass-Fed, Pasture-Raised, Dry-Aged and Organic under the menu-language section, and raw milk belongs there if anywhere, not in Dairy & Cheese. The question it answers (can a pregnant guest eat it, what does the 60-day rule mean) is a safety answer that every house trains as policy alongside allergens, and a vocabulary card is the wrong place to carry it. It also does not displace any of the four: a section holds at most four here and Raw Milk is behind Taleggio, Clothbound and Alpine-Style on the floor.

The menu prints the cheese, not the style: Humboldt Fog appears by name on American cheese courses far more often than the words ash-ripened or ashed, and the grey line is a detail the Bloomy Rind card already at Level 3 can carry in a clause (a layer of vegetable ash under the bloom, harmless, a tradition from Valencay). Adding a second card to explain one line of one cheese is not a Sous Chef word by the standard's signals, and the section is at its cap.

On an American menu raclette is a dish and an event before it is a cheese: raclette night, raclette over potatoes, a winter special for a few weeks a year. The guest's confusion with fondue is a confusion between two dishes, which is the preparations section's kind of card, not a dairy or cheese-course word; and at a good or fine-dining restaurant it is rarely on the menu at all. Not this section's word, and behind Taleggio for a slot in any case.

A fair style word and the next pick if the cap lifts, but it loses the fourth slot to Taleggio. On an American menu the guest meets Comte and Gruyere by name (and those are Level 1 to 2 words, outside this roster), while the printed word alpine-style appears only when the house serves an American-made alpine cheese, mostly on cheese courses at the top of the market. The Lexicon candidate alpage-cheeses-summer-milk holds it as a book entry about summer milk, which is a further sign it is read more than it is printed. Fewer menus and fewer guest questions than Taleggio, so it does not displace it.

Real and close, but the cap holds it out. Cheese courses print Cabot Clothbound as a proper name more than they print clothbound as a style word, and a Sous Chef answers the cloth in a clause (cheddar bandaged in cloth and lard and aged in a cave, so it dries and crumbles instead of staying waxy). It is on the cheese course only, where Taleggio is on savory plates every service; if the section ever takes a fifth Level III card, Clothbound and Alpine-Style are the next two.

A job title, not a menu word. The deck files its one job-title card, Garde Manger, under the menu-language section, and an affineur credit (selected by Herve Mons, aged by Jasper Hill Cellars) is printed on a handful of menus in the country at the very top of the market; the rule prefers words that appear on menus over words that appear in books, and this one appears mostly in books. If it is ever taught it belongs in the language section at Level 4, not here, and Robiola is this section's Level IV gain.

challenges.because: The proposer's own reason places it: it is the bread-service butter of nearly every ambitious American restaurant and is printed on the menu as house cultured butter, so a Chef de Partie server meets it every shift, not every month. It takes one sentence (cream ripened with live cultures before churning, so it tastes tangy), exactly the sentence the deck already gives Crème Fraîche at Level 2 and Buttermilk at Level 1, which are the same idea in cream and milk. By the standard's signals (on menus constantly, asked about at the first bread drop, one sentence to explain) it is Level 2, beside Crème Fraîche; the roster's aim of gaining Level III words does not make it a Level III word.

American cheese lists and carts print it as two words, triple crème, or in English as triple cream (Mt Tam, Kunik, Brillat-Savarin are all sold that way); the hyphen appears in French cheese writing, not on menus. Keep Triple Cream as the alias so the English printing matches too. The word itself, and Level 3 for it, are right: it is the third style word a server must read off a cheese course next to Bloomy Rind and Washed Rind, and no card or alias teaches it.

missing: Taleggio [3]: the one named washed-rind cheese on good and fine-dining American menus (pizza bianca, polenta, the cheese course), asked about every time because guests fear the smell; Washed Rind teaches the style, no card teaches the cheese servers actually sell

Raw Milk [3]: printed on every serious cheese list (raw cow's milk, raw sheep's milk) and the question pregnant guests and cautious guests ask first; the 60-day rule and pasteurized versus raw is a Sous Chef answer no card gives

Ash-Ripened [3]: the ashed goat cheeses that lead most American cheese courses (Humboldt Fog, Valençay style) print ash-ripened or ashed and the guest asks why there is a grey line through it; a style word on the course with no card

Raclette [3]: on menus as the cheese and as the dish (raclette over potatoes, raclette night), a name that means both the wheel and the scraping; asked about and confused with fondue, taught nowhere in the deck

Alpine-Style [3]: the style word for the Comté, Gruyère and Alpine cheeses that make up a third of an American cheese list; the Lexicon candidate alpage-cheeses-summer-milk holds it (alpage itself is the book word, alpine-style is the menu word)
Clothbound [3]: printed as clothbound cheddar on cheese courses at fine-dining houses and asked about (what is the cloth, why is it crumbly); a style word with no card

Affineur [4]: fine-dining cheese menus credit the affineur (cheeses selected by Hervé Mons, aged by Jasper Hill Cellars) and a senior server at the cart must explain what an affineur does; the rare, deeply specialist cheese-course word the Chef tier asks for
sections.note: Four proposals, three at Level III and one at Level IV. None of the brief's Lexicon candidates hold a dairy entry (alpage-cheeses-summer-milk is a seasonal-larder essay, not a menu word), so no lexiconSlug is given. Considered and set aside: Pecorino, Gruyère, Manchego, Halloumi and Labneh are Level II by the standard (common at a good restaurant, one sentence to explain); Ricotta Salata reads as a variant of the Ricotta card; Beurre Monté is real fine-dining butter vocabulary but menus print "butter-poached" far more often than the French, so Robiola took the Level IV seat.

proposals.reason: Unchallenged and it stands. Sardinian pasta of rolled, toasted semolina beads, printed as Fregola or Fregula, a fixture of fine-dining seafood and Italian menus (with clams, with 'nduja, under a whole fish) and confused by guests with Israeli or pearl couscous. The deck teaches Couscous at Level I and Semolina at Level II; fregola is the third of that family and the toasting is the point of the answer. Specialist product, on menus more than in books, needs a sentence: Level III.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is fregola a grain or a pasta? Is it like couscous?
proposals.menuLine: Fregola, Manila clams, 'nduja, preserved lemon, breadcrumbs

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list, the strongest of the pasta shapes named. Abruzzese fresh egg pasta cut on a wire-strung frame (the chitarra, a guitar) into square-sided strands, printed as Chitarra, Spaghetti alla Chitarra or Maccheroni alla Chitarra on fine-dining Italian and New American menus nationwide and almost never at casual rooms. The word is opaque to guests, who ask what it means and whether it is just spaghetti; the answer (a guitar, a wire frame, square strands that bite differently and hold sauce) is exactly the one-sentence fine-dining explanation Level III is for. The deck holds no square-cut or long fresh strand at any level.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does chitarra mean? Is it just spaghetti?
proposals.menuLine: Spaghetti alla chitarra, sea urchin, Calabrian chili, toasted breadcrumbs

proposals.reason: Moved from IV to III on the challenge. The heirloom long-grain rice of the Carolina Lowcountry, near-extinct by the 1920s and revived by seed growers and mills such as Anson Mills, now printed by name on good Southern menus weekly and already used as an example line under three other cards in this deck. It is a rice VARIETY, the analogue of Carnaroli (III), not a BRAND like Acquerello (IV); it sells to restaurants coast to coast; guests read it as a brand or a color and the answer is one sentence (heirloom Lowcountry long grain, aroma, separate grains); and the packet flag breaks ties downward. The Southern section that once held it was removed, so the deck no longer teaches it under any term.
proposals.guestsAsk: What makes Carolina Gold different from regular rice, and why is it named on the menu?
proposals.menuLine: Pan-roasted wreckfish, Carolina Gold rice, brown butter, field peas

proposals.reason: Operator ruling 27 Sep 2026: a rice VARIETY like Carnaroli (Level III), not a brand like Acquerello (Level IV); the roster's own Carolina Gold argument, and ties break down. Unchallenged and it stands. The short-grain Valencian paella rice, named on the menu wherever an American restaurant takes paella seriously (Jaleo, Boqueria, the wood-fired Spanish rooms) and usually sold with a 35 to 45 minute wait the server has to explain. Bomba drinks three times its volume of stock and stays in separate grains instead of going creamy, which is why it is not Arborio and why paella is never stirred. The deck holds Carnaroli at III and Acquerello at IV for the risotto side; bomba is the missing paella counterpart. Rare, specialist and tied to a classical dish: Level IV. The card's gist should name fideuà in one clause (the same pan with short noodles instead of rice).
proposals.guestsAsk: Why does it say Bomba rice, and why does the paella take forty minutes?
proposals.menuLine: Paella de mariscos, Bomba rice, head-on prawns, saffron, allioli, for two

dispositions.reason: The challenge is right. Level II in the standard is 'the main confusable pairs' and names Gnocchi as its example; gnudi is gnocchi's twin, on neighborhood Italian menus as well as fine-dining ones, and the answer is one sentence (ricotta, not potato). Its peers Agnolotti, Cavatelli and Orecchiette sit at II. Moved to Level II, which puts it outside this III/IV roster, so it is dropped here and flagged for the Level II gain pass: the deck should still teach it.

Moved from IV to III. It is a variety like Carnaroli (III), not a brand like Acquerello (IV); Anson Mills sells it coast to coast, good Southern menus print it weekly (the deck's own example lines under three other cards already do), the answer is one sentence, and the packet flag breaks ties downward. Level IV stays for the word a server meets a few times a year.

A real Level III word and the runner-up: Piedmontese thin egg ribbons, mistaken for tagliatelle. It does not make the list only because the roster caps at four and Chitarra outranks it on national menu frequency and on how often guests ask (tajarin clusters on Piedmontese and autumn truffle menus; chitarra is year-round across fine-dining Italian rooms). First in line if a slot opens.

Belongs to the section at Level III but ranks below Chitarra and Tajarin: it is printed less often on American fine-dining menus and guests ask less, since the plate makes the shape obvious and the penne confusion is settled by looking. No room within four.

Belongs to the section at Level III and is growing on fine-dining Italian menus, but it is newer and thinner on menus nationally than Chitarra, and the menu line usually says what is inside, so the guest's question is answered by the print. No room within four; a candidate for a later pass as it spreads.

A real word but its guest question ('is it tortellini?') is a one-clause confusable the Tortellini card (Level I) should carry in its gist rather than a card of its own; on American menus it is largely confined to cappelletti in brodo at serious Emilian rooms. Ranks below Chitarra and Tajarin; no room within four.

The gap in the farro family is real but the level is wrong for this roster: spelt is on bakery boards, brunch menus and grocery shelves everywhere, and the answer ('the third farro, farro grande') is one sentence, which is Level II by the standard (common at a good restaurant, needs a sentence).
