Dinkel is a book alias no American menu prints. Flagged for the Level II gain pass, ideally as a line in the Farro card's confusables.

After this roster the section names four rices (Arborio, Carnaroli, Acquerello, Bomba) plus Carolina Gold; a fifth Italian risotto rice that American menus print only occasionally is a book word more than a menu word, and the brief says prefer menus over books. The Carnaroli card can name it in a clause as the Venetian third.

Added at Level III as the missing list's strongest word: square-cut Abruzzese strands cut on a wire frame, on fine-dining Italian menus year-round, an opaque word guests ask about, and the deck holds no long fresh strand at any level. Printed as Chitarra, with Spaghetti alla Chitarra and Maccheroni alla Chitarra as the aliases the writer should carry.

Right word, wrong tier for this roster. Pici cacio e pepe and pici with ragu are now trattoria-common across the country; it is a peer of Cavatelli and Orecchiette (both Level II) and takes one sentence (hand-rolled thick Tuscan spaghetti, not udon). Level II by the standard, so outside a III/IV roster; flagged for the Level II gain pass.

Real and asked about, but wrong section. Bronze-die (bronze-cut, bronze-extruded) is a process credential printed the way Dry-Aged, House-Made and Heritage Breed are, and those live in the language section. This section holds grains, rice and pasta shapes, not credentials. Flagged for the language roster at Level III.

Not a shape of its own the section needs: it is the Gnocchi card's confusable (baked semolina disks, not potato) and belongs in that card's gist as one clause. Its own menu frequency in America is modest, well below the pasta shapes ranked above it.

Too rare on American menus to be a word a senior server must own; a handful of Sardinian-leaning rooms print it. Fregola carries the section's Sardinian flag and its card can name culurgiones as the neighbour. Prefer menus over books.

A dish rather than a grain or shape, and rarer than Bomba on the same menus. The guest's question (is it a typo for paella?) is answered in one clause, which the Bomba card should carry: the same pan with short noodles instead of rice.

Confined to a handful of Lowcountry rooms in the Husk line; the Carolina Gold card names the broken grains cooked like grits in one clause, and the Grits card (Level I) already covers the porridge the guest is comparing it to. Too narrow for a card of its own.

On menus it arrives as trofie al pesto, a line that explains itself, so guests rarely ask; the shape is a peer of Cavatelli (Level II) in frequency and difficulty, not a fine-dining word. Ranks below every pasta shape kept or listed above; no room within four.

challenges.because: Right word, wrong tier. The standard's own definition of Level II is 'the main confusable pairs' and names Gnocchi as the example; gnudi is gnocchi's twin and takes exactly one sentence (ricotta, not potato). It is on neighborhood Italian menus, not only fine-dining ones, and a Level II server at any Italian-leaning room meets it every week. The deck already places its peers Agnolotti, Cavatelli and Orecchiette at Level II; gnudi is no rarer than those. The proposer's 'Sous Chef-level vocabulary' is asserted, not shown.

A specialist product, not a rare one. It is a rice VARIETY, the analogue of Carnaroli (Level III), not a BRAND like Acquerello (Level IV); Anson Mills sells it to restaurants coast to coast and it is on good Southern menus weekly, which is why the deck's own example lines under three other cards already print it. Guests ask, the answer is one sentence (heirloom Lowcountry long grain, aroma, separate grains), and the packet flag breaks ties downward. Level III alongside Carnaroli; Level IV should stay for the word a server meets a few times a year.

missing: Tajarin [3]: Piedmontese thin egg noodles, on nearly every serious Italian menu under butter and truffle, mistaken for tagliatelle; the deck teaches Tagliatelle at II and nothing for its thinner northern cousin
Garganelli [3]: hand-rolled ridged egg-pasta quills, a fixture of fine-dining Italian menus, confused with penne
Caramelle [3]: candy-wrapper stuffed pasta, now on fine-dining Italian menus everywhere, guests ask what shape it is
Cappelletti [3]: little hats, the confusable twin of Tortellini (which the deck holds at I), printed in brodo and with brown butter

Spelt [3] (alias Farro Grande, Dinkel): the deck teaches Farro as emmer and Farro Piccolo as einkorn but not the third farro; spelt is on menus as spelt salad, spelt bread, spelt risotto and guests ask if it is farro
Vialone Nano [4]: the third risotto rice, Venetian, printed by name at serious Italian rooms; completes the Arborio/Carnaroli/Acquerello set the section already builds
Spaghetti alla Chitarra [3] (menus print Chitarra): square-cut Abruzzese strands cut on a wire frame, on fine-dining Italian menus, guests ask what chitarra means
Pici [3]: Tuscan hand-rolled thick spaghetti, printed as pici with ragù or cacio e pepe, guests ask if it is udon
Bronze-Die [3] (alias Bronze-Cut, Bronze-Extruded): printed on menus as a pasta credential; guests ask what it means and the answer (rough surface holds sauce) is one sentence
Gnocchi alla Romana [3]: baked semolina disks, not potato; the confusable cousin of the Gnocchi card, on fine-dining and trattoria menus
Culurgiones [4]: pleated Sardinian potato-and-mint dumplings, rare but printed by name where fregola is
Fideuà [4]: paella made with short noodles instead of rice, on the same Spanish menus that print Bomba, guests assume a typo for paella
Rice Middlins [4] (alias Rice Grits, Broken Rice): the broken Carolina Gold grains cooked like grits, printed at Husk-line Southern rooms, guests read it as a misprint
Trofie [3]: Ligurian hand-rolled twists, the pasta menus pair with pesto by name
sections.note: Four proposals, two at each level, all confirmed absent from everyCard (term and alias) and from the Lexicon's terms and slugs, so no lexiconSlug applies. Verified against the built deck too: Carolina Gold appears there only inside example menu lines of other cards (Andouille, Crawfish, Wreckfish), never as a taught term, and its old Southern card fd_0018 was removed with that section. None of the brief's Lexicon candidates belongs to this section. Runners-up if the reconciler wants more or wants to swap: Pici (III, hand-rolled Tuscan strands, everywhere now with cacio e pepe), Garganelli (III, hand-rolled ridged egg tubes), Spaghetti alla Chitarra (III), Paccheri (III), Spelt (III, the farro grande that completes the Farro / Farro Piccolo trio), Vialone Nano (IV, the third risotto rice). Left out on purpose: Bucatini, Masa, Soba and Spaetzle, which are Level II by the standard, and Tortelloni and Raviolo, which the spelling-variant rule would catch.

proposals.reason: The steakhouse sauce at nearly every good American beef house: a red-wine and shallot reduction built on demi-glace, classically finished with poached bone marrow. The deck teaches Demi-Glace (2) and Bone Marrow (meats, 2) but not the sauce that joins them; a named classical child of the brown sauce that a server explains in one sentence, which is the Level III standard (classical sauces and preparations). Not a Level IV word: it is on too many menus for a senior server to be the only one who owns it.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is bordelaise, and is there actually marrow in it?
proposals.menuLine: Dry-Aged New York Strip, Bone Marrow Bordelaise, Pommes Purée

proposals.reason: The cold classical egg sauce built on hard-cooked yolks rather than raw ones, mashed with mustard and oil and sharpened with cornichon, capers and herbs; printed under asparagus, sweetbreads, fried fish and tête de veau at fine-dining restaurants. It sits beside Remoulade (2) as its confusable but adds a mechanism the deck lacks (a cooked-yolk emulsion), and the egg question comes up every night it runs. Fine-dining vocabulary with a classical pedigree: Level III.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is gribiche like tartar sauce, and does it have raw egg in it?
proposals.menuLine: Grilled Green Asparagus, Sauce Gribiche, Soft Herbs, Brioche Crumb

proposals.reason: The onion sauce of the classical repertoire: onions sweated to sweetness and bound with béchamel or cream, today printed on its own as an onion soubise under lamb, pork chop, chicken and roasted alliums at fine-dining and ambitious neighborhood restaurants. The deck has Béchamel (2) but not this child of it, and the word tells a guest nothing on its own; a dairy question rides with it. Classical mother-sauce child that needs explaining: Level III.
proposals.guestsAsk: What's a soubise?
proposals.menuLine: Roasted Pork Chop, Onion Soubise, Charred Spring Onions, Mustard Jus

proposals.reason: The aromatic court-bouillon a shellfish or fish is poached in and then served in, so the dish arrives 'à la nage', swimming; a deeply classical French stock word that fine-dining menus still print for lobster, langoustine, scallops and halibut. It is a stock served as the sauce, the exact seam of this section, and rare enough that only a senior server owns it: Level IV, where the section held no card at all. It takes the Level IV stock slot ahead of Fumet because menus print it and Fumet stays in books.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does 'à la nage' mean, is it a soup or a sauce?
proposals.menuLine: Butter-Poached Maine Lobster à la Nage, Fennel, Champagne Grapes

dispositions.reason: A real fine-dining word and the first alternate if the owner wants a fifth card, but the section is at its cap of four and this is the one a server can already bridge from a card in hand: it is a warm tomato-herb vinaigrette, and Vinaigrette (1) sits in this section. Each of the four kept words adds a mechanism the deck lacks (demi-glace child, cooked-yolk emulsion, béchamel child, stock served as sauce); Sauce Vierge adds none.

Taught adjacent already: the deck holds Aioli (2) and Bouillabaisse (preparations, 3), and rouille is explained on the floor in five words as the saffron-chile aioli that comes with the bouillabaisse. On American menus it is printed almost only as that garnish, never on its own, so it rides on the Bouillabaisse card rather than earning one.

On American menus it is printed almost only inside the dish name Vitello Tonnato, which a server learns as the dish, not as a sauce; where it does travel (chicken tonnato, tonnato with roasted vegetables) it is a mayonnaise variant a server bridges from Aioli (2) and Remoulade (2). The section's cold-emulsion gain is Gribiche, which adds a mechanism; Tonnato would be a second cold mayonnaise under the cap.

Wrong section and thin on menus: where it appears it is printed as a dish, a warm anchovy-garlic dip with crudités, so it is a preparation, not a mother sauce, emulsion, stock or cold sauce as the blurb defines this section. Rare on American menus outside Piedmont-leaning Italian rooms; prefer menu words over book words.

It belongs to this section (a stock) and servers do need it, but not at the level the roster gains. Wrong section: a jarred dried-seafood condiment, the peer of Miso (pantry, 2) and Fish Sauce (pantry, 2), which the deck files under Pantry; nothing in the blurb (mother sauces, emulsions, stocks, cold sauces) holds it. A marinade and herb condiment whose nearest cards are Chimichurri (2) and Salsa Verde (2); by the deck's placements it sits at Level II, below what this roster gains, and on American menus it is printed as a marinade on the protein more than as a sauce. proposals.reason: The section's blurb promises 'baked under a crust' and the deck has no card for the phrase menus actually print. Common at fine dining, rare at casual, a sentence to explain: Level III. A dish name that is really an instruction, so it belongs here rather than in custards or menu language. Needs a sentence to carry both meanings and is fine-dining vocabulary, which is Level III by the standard. No card, term or alias anywhere in the deck covers it.

dispositions.reason: Added at Level 3. Dropped from the proposer's list to make room for Quenelle. Raw is already the section's heaviest lane (Carpaccio, Tartare, Crudo, Ceviche, Tataki), the guest's question is answered in a clause against Ceviche at II, and it is met mainly at coastal and Mexican-leaning houses, where Quenelle is met at every fine-dining dessert course. It is the first reserve if the cap ever moves to five.

A real fine-dining word and the cured half of the blurb, but the slate is full at four and it sits below Torchon, Quenelle and En Croûte on how often it is printed and asked about on American menus. Second reserve after Aguachile.

A home-cooking and bistro word rarely printed at good American restaurants; the guest's 'is it a stew?' is answered from Ragout at II, and a card would repeat that gist with 'not browned first'. Book word over menu word.

A named French dish rarely printed on American menus; a server meets it in books and in France, not on the floor. Cassoulet and Bouillabaisse earned their cards on frequency; this one does not clear that bar.

Tonnato is a sauce (tuna, anchovy and caper mayonnaise) and belongs in Sauces & Condiments beside Aioli and Remoulade; vitello is only its classic carrier, and menus now print 'tonnato' on vegetables and other meats. Not a preparation or style word for this section.

The Italian name for the rolled-and-stuffed preparation Roulade already teaches at II; a card would repeat Roulade's gist with an Italian label. If the word needs to be searchable, it is an alias on Roulade, not a new card.

Means 'with onions' and is printed on potatoes and one salad; a one-word gloss rather than a preparation that needs a card, and modest in frequency on American menus. Below the four kept words on every signal.

It is the gratin the deck already teaches at I, with potato and cream named; the guest's 'is it scalloped potatoes?' is answered by the Gratin card's gist. At most an alias on Gratin, not a Level III card.

Raw is already the section's heaviest lane with five cards, and tiradito lives at Peruvian and Nikkei houses; even Aguachile, far more common on American menus, did not hold a slot. A word for the Lexicon, not the floor deck.

En Croûte carries the blurb's 'baked under a crust'; Pithivier is one form of it, printed at a handful of tasting-menu houses. A book word more than a menu word, and the section does not need two crust cards.

A charcuterie item (sausage patty wrapped in caul fat) that belongs in Cured & Charcuterie beside Andouille, Pâté and Terrine, not a style word for this section; and it is rarely printed at all on American menus.
A classical kitchen term met in books; American menus print 'in its broth' or 'in nage' seldom enough that a server will not be asked about it. Book word over menu word, and the slate is full.

A named French dish rarely printed on American menus; its white-stew explanation rests on Velouté, already taught in Sauces. Level IV is for the rare word a senior server must own because they will meet it; this one they largely will not.

proposals.reason: A nut meringue baked as a layer, printed as 'hazelnut dacquoise' or 'almond dacquoise' on fine-dining dessert cards as the base or tier of a plated cake. It sounds like a place or a sauce, it hides a tree-nut allergen behind a French word, and a server must hold three ideas at once: it is a meringue, it is a nut meringue, and it is a layer rather than a shell. The deck teaches Meringue (fd_0240, Level 1) and Pavlova (fd_0247, Level 2); this is the classical construction beyond them, and the section held no Level IV card. Chef by the 'deeply classical word a senior server must own' clause. Uncontested by the challenger.

proposals.reason: The small fluted Bordeaux pastry with a dark, near-bitter caramelized crust and a soft custardy rum-vanilla inside, served warm as a mignardise or with coffee at most tasting-menu restaurants in the United States. Guests ask whether it is burnt every night it is served; the answer needs a real sentence (a crêpe-like batter baked in beeswax-lined copper molds so the outside caramelizes while the inside stays custard). Common enough on the floor that a Level III server meets it weekly, which is Sous Chef rather than Chef. Not covered by Custard (fd_0250) or any bread card. Uncontested by the challenger.

proposals.reason: The laminated Breton butter pastry: croissant-style dough folded with sugar and salted butter and baked until the sugar caramelizes into a shattering shell. It has crossed from bakeries onto bread service, brunch and dessert menus at good American restaurants, and where it is served the floor meets it every shift and guests ask every time, mostly how to say it. The explanation is one sentence built on a Level 1 card, Puff Pastry (fd_0244), plus caramelized sugar, which places it beside Pâte à Choux (fd_0243) and Clafoutis (fd_0245) at Sous Chef, not with Acquerello and Ballotine at Chef. The Lexicon's 'lamination' candidate is the mechanism, not the menu word. Moved from Level 4 to Level 3 on the challenge.

proposals.reason: The salted-butter Breton shortbread, printed as 'sablé' or 'sablé breton' (alias) on fine-dining dessert cards as the crisp base under fruit, cream or ice cream, and as a cookie among the mignardises. It is on more tasting-menu dessert cards than any other word in this batch, guests ask 'what is a sablé' because nothing on the menu glosses it, and the deck has no cookie, shortbread or short-crust card to explain it from. One sentence to explain (a crumbly salted-butter shortbread from Brittany, 'sablé' meaning sandy), which is Sous Chef by the standard. Added from the challenger's list; it takes the fourth seat over Financier, which is explainable from Brown Butter (fd_0161) and Torte (fd_0242) and is printed less often on the dinner dessert card.

The Level IV clause is for the rare specialist or deeply classical word (Acquerello, Banyuls, Ballotine); a Breton pastry that is now a trend item on American brunch and bread-service menus is Sous Chef vocabulary beside Pâte à Choux and Clafoutis. Dropped by the reconciler, not by a challenge, to hold the section at four. It is a good word (brown-butter almond cake, an allergen question, a mignardise at many fine-dining tables) but it is the one proposal a server can half-build from cards the deck already holds, Brown Butter (fd_0161) and Torte (fd_0242), and it is printed on the dinner dessert card less often than Sablé, which takes its seat. Financier is first in line if the section cap lifts or the deck needs more Level III cards.

Added at Level 3, with the card term shortened to 'Sablé' because menus print both 'sablé' and 'sablé breton'; 'Sablé Breton' is the alias. It is the most frequently printed word on tasting-menu dessert cards among everything named here, guests ask because no menu glosses it, and nothing in the deck (no cookie, shortbread or short-crust card) explains it. Does not earn a seat under the cap. A real menu word with a real allergen question, but it does not belong to THIS section. Frangipane is an almond cream, a filling baked into a tart; the deck files creams and fillings under Custards, Creams & Frozen (Pastry Cream fd_0264, Ganache fd_0251, Chantilly fd_0265), not under doughs and batters. It should be proposed to the custards roster at Level 3, where 'pear frangipane tart' and 'does it have nuts' are exactly the floor question. A named choux dish, but the deck's Pâte à Choux card (fd_0243, Level 3, alias Choux) already teaches 'hollow shells to fill', and a Paris-Brest is that shell as a ring with praline cream, one clause on an existing Level III card. It is a fixture only at French-leaning fine dining in the United States, which puts it below Canelé, Kouign-Amann and Sablé on the frequency signal, and the section cap is four. If the deck wants a second choux dish, Gougère is the more frequent one.

Served nightly at French restaurants as the amuse or the bread, and printed on bistro snack menus, so it is a legitimate floor word; but it is one sentence from Pâte à Choux (fd_0243, Level 3): the same dough with cheese folded in, baked as a puff, not filled. Its frequency is house-specific (French rooms) rather than deck-wide, and under a cap of four it loses to Canelé and Sablé, which appear at tasting-menu restaurants of every cuisine. First in line among the choux dishes if the section grows.

Deeply classical and a true Level IV word by the clause, but it appears on a handful of classical French menus in the United States (Daniel, Le Bernardin) and almost nowhere else, which fails the 'prefer words that appear on menus' rule against Dacquoise, which is on fine-dining dessert cards nationwide and already holds the section's Level IV seat. Not covered by any deck card; it is the next Level IV for this section if the cap lifts or the deck needs more Chef cards, and the tableside rum pour and 'how boozy is it' are the right card.

The best-argued of the missing words and the one honest second Level IV here: a pastry-kitchen component printed as 'praline feuilletine' that nobody outside pastry knows, with a hidden wheat question under a name that guests read as nuts, and a sound-alike trap against the deck's Pâte Feuilletée alias. Rejected under the cap on the standard's own signals: it is a garnish component rather than a dough or dish, it is printed less often than Sablé, and guests rarely ask about it by name, they ask about the praline. If the section takes a fifth card or the deck needs Level IV cards to reach the minimum, Feuilletine at Level 4 is the one to add, with the gluten point written into the card.

proposals.reason: The classical warm foam of yolks whisked with wine or Champagne over a bain-marie: a custard by definition, served warm, aerated and carrying alcohol (Marsala, Champagne, Sauternes), which is what surprises guests who expect a cold cream. Fine-dining dessert menus print it as Sabayon over berries or as the sauce under a fruit gratin; Italian menus print only Zabaglione or Zabaione, so the card carries both as aliases (challenger's note accepted). Level 3 by the standard: fine-dining and classical, asked about, one sentence to explain, and the warm wine-based cousin a Sous Chef-level server tells apart from Crème Anglaise. Not in the deck under any term or alias.

It belongs with Puff Pastry, Pâte à Choux and Meringue in the pastry section, where it should be re-proposed at Level 4 with the same menu line and gluten question.

Dropped. On American menus 'Bavarois' turns up on a handful of classical French cards and 'Bavarian cream' at the doughnut counter, where no guest asks; the brief says prefer menu words over book words, and the Level 4 examples (Bottarga, Ballotine, Banyuls) are rare but live. Crémeux already gives the section its gelatin-set anglaise, and Vacherin now fills the Chef level with a word that is actually printed.

Added at Level 3. Lemon posset is on good and fine-dining American dessert menus every season, guests ask what it is, and a citrus-set cream with no egg and no gelatin is the sharpest 'told apart by what goes in it' card the section lacked.

Added, moved from the challenger's 3 to 4. It is a frozen dessert on fine-dining menus and a confusable with the washed-rind cheese the deck already teaches at Level 4; rarer on menus than the three Level 3 words and harder to explain because the word has two meanings, which by the signals is the Chef standard. The dish is poached meringue; the crème anglaise beneath it is already taught in this section at Level 2. Gianduja is a chocolate-hazelnut paste, a flavour and an ingredient rather than a set preparation; on menus it rides on a form the deck already teaches (gianduja mousse, gianduja crémeux). The section's four slots go to set preparations, and Posset and Vacherin are the stronger cards. A fair candidate for a chocolate or pantry pass later.

A pastry-kitchen word that appears on very few American menus; by the challenger's own menu-over-book standard it is rarer in print than Bavarois. Crémeux covers the set chocolate cream a server will actually be asked about.

Pastry cream folded with whipped cream is the combination of two cards the deck already holds, Pastry Cream (alias Crème Pâtissière) and Chantilly, so a server who knows both can answer it. On menus it appears as 'diplomat cream' inside a tart description where guests seldom ask. Not a Level 4 word a senior server must own beyond those two cards.

A frozen soufflé is a parfait or semifreddo base set in a collared ramekin to stand above the rim; the deck teaches Parfait and Semifreddo, and the word is rarely printed on American menus today. The confusion with the baked Soufflé card is real but belongs in that card's text, not a new card.

Budino stands, but not in this roster: butterscotch budino is on so many Italian-American menus and takes one sentence to explain ('Italian pudding, a soft custard'), which is the Level 2 standard (Gelato, Macaron), not Level 3. Flagged for the owner as a Level 2 hole in this section.

Out of this roster's levels, which gain only at Level III and IV. The challenger is right that both are first-week words the deck does not teach (Flan / Crème Caramel at 1, Affogato at 2); flagged for the owner as the section's two largest Level 1 and 2 holes.
Sabayon stands and the card carries Zabaglione and Zabaione as aliases, since Italian menus print only those; the alias note is written into the Sabayon proposal.

challenges.because: Wrong section. Feuilletine is a crisp crêpe-dentelle wafer, a baked crumb: nothing in it is set with egg, cream, gelatin or cold, so it fails this section's own blurb. It belongs with Puff Pastry, Pâte à Choux and Meringue in the pastry section, where it should be re-proposed at Level 4 (the menu line and the gluten question are sound there). Keeping it here teaches a server that a wafer is a custard.

A book word on American menus. In twenty years the word 'bavarois' turns up on a handful of classical French cards; 'Bavarian cream' turns up at the doughnut counter, where no guest asks anything. The brief says prefer menu words over book words, and the Level 4 examples (Bottarga, Ballotine, Banyuls) are rare but live on menus; this one is rare and mostly in Escoffier. Crémeux already gives the section its gelatin-set anglaise. If the reconciler wants a second classical set cream, Crème Diplomat is printed more often today than Bavarois.

missing: Posset [3]: lemon posset is on good and fine-dining American dessert menus every season, a citrus-set cream with no egg and no gelatin, and 'what is a posset?' is asked at every table; it is the cleanest 'told apart by what goes in it' card the section lacks
Île Flottante [3]: printed as Île Flottante or Floating Island on bistro and fine-dining menus, poached meringue on crème anglaise; guests ask what it is; not taught by the Meringue card
Gianduja [3]: hazelnut-chocolate paste, printed on plated desserts (gianduja mousse, gianduja crémeux) and asked about; the chocolate-work word the section's blurb promises and does not hold

Vacherin [3]: meringue shell with ice cream and cream, on fine-dining dessert menus, and a confusable with the washed-rind cheese of the same name, which is exactly the pairing a Sous Chef-level server owns
Namelaka [4]: the Japanese-French set chocolate cream now printed on tasting menus; rare, specialist, nobody at the table knows it
Crème Diplomat [4]: pastry cream folded with whipped cream, printed as 'diplomat cream' in tarts and choux on fine pastry menus; the classical set cream that is actually on menus today
Soufflé Glacé [4]: frozen soufflé, deeply classical, still printed in classical French rooms and confused with the baked Soufflé card
Budino [3, on the seam with II]: butterscotch budino is on half the Italian-American menus in the country and guests ask every night; not in the deck under any term
Note, outside this roster's levels: Flan / Crème Caramel [1] and Affogato [2] are the section's largest holes; a server meets both in the first week and the deck teaches neither
Note: Sabayon stands, but the card needs 'Zabaglione' (and 'Zabaione') as aliases, since Italian menus print only that
sections.note: None of the brief's Lexicon candidates belong to this section (no dessert entries among them), so no proposal carries a lexiconSlug; each term was also grepped across tools/deck and the deck modules and none exists under any term, alias or spelling variant (the words appear only in recipe data, never in a card). Runners-up considered and left out: Budino (very common on good American menus, but that commonness places it at Level II beside Panna Cotta and Pot de Crème, not III); Gianduja and Posset (honest Level III words, and the strongest substitutes if the operator wants a different pair at III); Namelaka and Dulcey (Level IV chocolate work, but book-and-pastry-lab words more than menu words). Île Flottante was passed over because its identity is the meringue, which the deck already teaches in the bread section.

proposals.reason: The Basque PDO chili, dried and ground, mild and fruity with a slow warmth; fine-dining kitchens print it by name over fish, eggs and butter sauces where a bistro would write 'paprika'. Renamed from the proposer's 'Piment d'Espelette' because American menus print the short form ('espelette aioli', 'octopus, espelette'); the card should carry 'Piment d'Espelette' and 'Espelette Pepper' as aliases so a study search on any of the three lands. Taught nowhere in the deck under any term or alias; Pimentón (Level II) is Spanish smoked paprika, a different pepper, and the pair is worth teaching against each other. Fine-dining vocabulary that needs a sentence, so Sous Chef by the standard, beside Mostarda and Beurre Blanc.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is Espelette spicy? Is it like paprika or cayenne?
proposals.menuLine: Halibut, brown butter, espelette, sweet corn

proposals.reason: A Japanese fermented paste of green chili, yuzu zest and salt, dotted on crudo, oysters and grilled fish across American fine dining today; unchallenged and it stands. The deck teaches neither yuzu nor kosho under any term or alias (the Lexicon has the yuzu fruit alone, no kosho), and it is the pantry word most often printed beside a raw-fish course. Guests ask what it is and whether it is hot, and answering takes a sentence about fermentation and citrus, which places it at Sous Chef rather than Chef; it is too common now for Level IV.
proposals.guestsAsk: What is yuzu kosho, and is it spicy?
proposals.menuLine: Hamachi crudo, yuzu kosho, cucumber, shiso oil

proposals.reason: Added from the challenger's missing list. Whole heads held warm and humid for weeks until the cloves turn soft, black and balsamic-sweet; it is on fine-dining menus constantly, and the deck already prints it in its own Abalone Mushroom menu line (mushrooms.mjs line 21) without teaching it, the same untaught-in-our-own-line fault the challenger found with quince paste. The Lexicon's entry settles the guest question in one line: aged, not fermented, and not burnt. Belongs to this section under 'ferments and the seasonings that finish a plate', taught under no term or alias, and it needs a sentence, so Sous Chef. It takes the fourth seat over Quince Paste because it is on more menus and draws the question more often.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is black garlic burnt? Is it fermented? Does it taste like garlic?
proposals.menuLine: Roasted carrots, black garlic, whipped ricotta, hazelnut

dispositions.reason: Renamed to Espelette at Level 3. The challenger is right that American fine-dining menus print the short form far more often than the PDO label; 'Piment d'Espelette' and 'Espelette Pepper' go on the card as aliases so either spelling resolves in a study search.

The rename to Quince Paste is right on the merits (verified: dairy.mjs line 18 prints 'quince paste', and the deck's pattern is English term with the foreign alias, as Fish Sauce/Nam Pla and Brown Butter/Beurre Noisette), but the card is dropped rather than renamed. The section is capped at four, and once the term is the plain English phrase, the how-often-guests-ask signal falls below Black Garlic's, which is on more menus and is also printed untaught in the deck's own Abalone Mushroom line. If the owner later widens the section, Quince Paste (aliases Membrillo, Dulce de Membrillo) at Level 3 is the next card in.

Added at Level 3, taking the fourth seat. Constantly on fine-dining menus, printed in the deck's own mushrooms.mjs line 21 without a card, draws the burnt-or-fermented question every service, and belongs to the section's 'ferments and the seasonings that finish a plate'. The Lexicon holds it in the Vegetable Atlas with no Level III/IV placement, so it is not among the brief's candidates and no slug is cited.

A real fine-dining word and the fish-allergy flag is a fair point, but the deck teaches the product class under Fish Sauce (Level 2), and the Italian anchovy drip is better carried as an alias and a sentence on that card than as a fifth pantry card; it appears on far fewer American menus than the four kept.

Good-restaurant word with a live nut-allergy question, but it loses the seat count to Black Garlic, Espelette and Yuzu Kosho on menu frequency, and the deck has no other Levantine or Egyptian pantry card for it to pair against. First reserve if the owner raises the cap.

On menus at good restaurants and it hides fish, but it is a garnish shake that the Japanese words already kept (Yuzu Kosho, Koji) outrank on frequency at fine dining and on how much it takes to explain; four is the cap and it does not displace any of them.

The name explains itself on the menu: a guest reads 'pomegranate' and 'molasses' and asks only whether it is sweet, a one-word answer. The standard weights how much a word takes to explain, and this one takes almost nothing, so it does not earn a Level III card.

Printed by name on lamb, carrots and couscous and guests do ask if it is hot, but it is a blend whose contents vary house to house, so the card could only teach 'a North African spice blend'; against the cap it loses to words with a single teachable answer.

The 'confusable beside Aleppo' argument fails because Aleppo is not in the deck under any term or alias either; a confusable pair needs both halves. The Lexicon holds Urfa Biber, but 'urfa' alone appears on fewer American menus than Espelette, which fills the dried-chile seat.

A genuine Level IV fine-dining word, but it appears on fewer menus than Koji, which takes the section's one new Chef seat and also deepens the existing Miso card. Next Level IV reserve for this section.

Seen on fine-dining crudo and vegetable courses, and 'plum or pickle' is a real question, but the section already carries a Japanese ferment at each new level (Yuzu Kosho at III, Koji at IV) and four is the cap; it does not outrank either on frequency.

A book word more than a menu word: American menus print 'Moscatel vinegar' rarely, and when they do the guest question is the same one the Banyuls card (Level 4) already answers about a sweet-grape vinegar. The brief prefers words that appear on menus over words that appear in books, and Banyuls already holds that seat.

challenges.because: Right word, right level, but American menus print the short form: 'grilled octopus, espelette', 'espelette aioli', 'espelette, brown butter'. The full 'piment d'Espelette' is the label on the jar and the PDO name, and it is what a French bistro prints; the server scanning a fine-dining menu meets 'Espelette' alone far more often. Term should be Espelette with 'Piment d'Espelette' and 'Espelette Pepper' as aliases, so a study search on either lands.

Right product, right level, but at a good or fine-dining American restaurant the cheese course prints 'quince paste' at least as often as 'membrillo', and the deck already does exactly that: dairy.mjs line 18 pairs a cheese with 'Black cherry jam, quince paste, walnuts, crusty bread'. A card whose term disagrees with the deck's own menu line teaches the wrong reflex. Term Quince Paste, alias Membrillo (and Dulce de Membrillo), so the Spanish-menu case is still covered and the guest question 'what is membrillo' still resolves.

missing: Black Garlic [3] (aged whole heads, sweet and balsamic-dark; on fine-dining menus constantly and already printed in the deck's own Abalone Mushroom line without being taught; guests ask if it is burnt or fermented)
Colatura [4] (colatura di alici, the Italian anchovy drip; fine-dining pasta courses print it by name; Fish Sauce card covers nam pla and nuoc mam, not this; fish allergy flag)
Dukkah [3] (Egyptian nut, seed and spice crumble scattered over vegetables and labneh at good restaurants; nut allergy question every time)
Furikake [3] (Japanese seaweed-sesame-bonito shake, now on fries, rice and fish at good restaurants; hides fish, so the guest question is an allergy question)
Pomegranate Molasses [3] (reduced pomegranate juice, tart and syrupy; printed on Levantine-leaning menus beside labneh, eggplant and lamb; guests ask if it is sweet)
Ras el Hanout [3] (North African 'top of the shop' blend; printed by name on lamb, carrots and couscous; guests ask if it is hot)
Urfa Biber [3] (Turkish dried chile, smoky and raisin-dark, mild; menus print 'urfa' alone; the confusable beside Aleppo)
Vadouvan [4] (French-Indian curry blend with shallot and garlic; fine-dining word on carrots, cauliflower and fish; guests ask if it is curry)
Umeboshi [4] (Japanese salt-cured sour plum and its paste; fine-dining crudo and vegetable courses; guests ask if it is a plum or a pickle)
Moscatel Vinegar [4] (sweet Spanish grape vinegar from Moscatel, the sibling of Banyuls on fine-dining vinaigrettes; the card the Banyuls card asks for)
sections.note: Four proposals, none from the Lexicon candidates (no candidate belongs to Pantry; Seville Orange, Asafoetida and Panch Phoron are fruit and spice entries, not jars). Checked every term and alias in everyCard: none of Espelette, yuzu, kosho, quince, membrillo or koji appears, and none is a spelling variant of a held card. Considered and left out: Colatura di Alici (Italian anchovy drippings, a fair Level IV on Italian fine-dining menus but close in kind to the Fish Sauce card and asked about less often than the four above); Black Garlic, Gochujang and Aleppo Pepper (all on menus, but common enough at good restaurants to sit at Level II by the standard, like Pimentón); Fleur de Sel and Vincotto (too near Finishing Salt and Saba); Salsa Macha and XO (condiments, but they read as sauces and belong to that section). If the deck wants a fifth, Colatura at Level IV is the honest next word.

proposals.reason: The closing counterpart to Amuse-Bouche (Level II in this section): the tray of tiny sweets that arrives after dessert, printed as the last line of the tasting menu at every tasting-menu house in America and said at every table there every night. That is the definition of fine-dining vocabulary (Level III), not the rare word a senior server meets a few times a year (Level IV, beside Acquerello and Ballotine), so the challenger's move is accepted. One sentence explains it: included in the menu price, not a course you order, sometimes sent with coffee. The card carries Petits Fours as an alias, because half the houses print that instead. Neither word is in everyCard.
proposals.guestsAsk: What are mignardises, is that another dessert, and are they included in the menu price?
proposals.menuLine: Coffee or tea, and mignardises for the table

proposals.reason: A handling claim now printed on fish courses at the best American restaurants (ikejime madai, ikejime hiramasa) and exactly what the blurb says this section holds: what the claim means and what it does not. It means the fish was spike-killed and bled at the boat so stress chemistry and rigor are delayed and the flesh stays clear and firm for days; it is not a species, a grade, a freshness date, or a promise the fish was caught nearby. Rare, Japanese, and a paragraph to explain: Level IV by the standard, beside Bottarga and Lion's Mane, and the section's first Level IV card. Unchallenged; not in everyCard.
proposals.guestsAsk: What does ikejime mean, is that a kind of fish?
proposals.menuLine: Ikejime madai crudo, finger lime, shiso oil

proposals.reason: The sourcing claim that has replaced sustainable on good and fine-dining menus (regeneratively raised beef, from regenerative farms). Unlike Organic (Level I here) it has no federal definition; only the private Regenerative Organic Certified mark is audited, so the server must say what the house is actually claiming (grazing and cropping that rebuild soil and hold carbon) and what it does not guarantee (grass-finished, organic, or pasture-raised). Common enough at fine dining, needs more than a sentence, and its nuance sits above Grass-Fed (I) and Pasture-Raised (II): Level III. Unchallenged; not in everyCard.
proposals.guestsAsk: Regenerative, is that the same thing as organic or grass-fed?
proposals.menuLine: Dry-aged ribeye, regeneratively raised, White Oak Pastures, GA

proposals.reason: The third menu structure after Prix Fixe and Tasting Menu (both Level I): printed at every sushi counter and at Japanese-leaning fine dining, and borrowed loosely by other houses. It means I leave it to you: the chef decides course by course, usually at the counter, sized to the diner and the day's fish, priced by tier or at market, with the guest expected to name dislikes up front and add-ons offered at the end. Not an alias of Tasting Menu (fd_0290 carries Degustation and Chef's Tasting) and it behaves differently. At a sushi house it is day-one vocabulary, but at a good or fine-dining American restaurant it is the word a guest brings from elsewhere and asks the server to compare against the house tasting, and the answer takes more than a sentence: Level III. Added from the challenger's missing list; not in everyCard.
proposals.guestsAsk: Is the omakase a set number of courses, do we get to choose anything, and is the price fixed?
proposals.menuLine: Omakase   18 courses at the counter   225 per person

dispositions.reason: Moved to Level II and therefore dropped from this roster, which gains only Level III and IV words. The challenger is right on the facts: Restaurant Week cards, brunch prix fixe and bistro set menus across America print 'supplement 12' or '(+$10 supplement)', so a Level II server meets the word weekly, and the explanation is one sentence (an add-on charged on top of the set price, per person unless it says for the table). That is the Chef de Partie standard exactly, and it sits by parity with Amuse-Bouche (II). It is a good card for a later Level II pass beside Prix Fixe, not a Sous Chef word.

Moved from Level IV to Level III and kept. It is printed on the last line of every tasting menu at every tasting-menu house and said nightly at every table there: fine-dining vocabulary by the standard, not the rare word of Level IV. Petits Fours added as an alias on the card, since half the houses print that instead; it is not in everyCard.

Added at Level III. A printed menu-structure word, not an alias of Tasting Menu (fd_0290 carries Degustation and Chef's Tasting), and it behaves differently: ordered at the counter, sized by the chef, priced by tier or at market. Guests ask whether they choose, how many courses, and whether the price is fixed, and the answer takes more than a sentence. It belongs to the blurb's first clause, how a menu is structured, where the section had nothing above Level I.

On food menus it is rare; where a server meets it nightly is the wine list, and that is the Sommelier's Codex's word to teach, not the World Table's. The one private-standard sourcing claim this section needs beyond Organic is Regenerative, which is what American menus now print on the meat and produce lines, and a two-to-four-card roster cannot carry two private-certification claims when only one of them is a food-menu word. Biodynamic does not belong on this roster.

A real menu word, but Level II by the deck's own parity: Day-Boat (fd_0299) is a Level II claim of the same kind (how the fish came in), met at the same good seafood restaurants at the same frequency, and explained in the same one sentence (taken one at a time on a hook, so it is a method, not a freshness date or a location, and implies wild). The challenger placed it above Day-Boat because it is the third confusable, but a third confusable is not a higher one. It belongs beside Day-Boat in a Level II pass, not on a Level III and IV roster.

Fine-dining vocabulary, but it fails the signals for Level III: American tasting menus now mostly print the item (a granita, a sorbet) and announce the course, so the word is heard more than read; the explanation is one clause (a palate cleanser between savory and sweet, not a dessert); and the food that lands is already taught (Granita fd_0257, Sorbet fd_0259). Mignardises takes the structural Level III slot because it is printed at every tasting house and asked about at every table. Intermezzo is a Level II word for a later pass.

Printed at the foot of the menu, but guests almost never ask what it means; they ask who the chef is and get a name. The blurb's 'kitchen stations' are the posts on the line (Garde Manger, Saucier, Pâtissier), and a title is not a station. By the roster's rule, prefer words on menus over words in books, this is a book word about the brigade rather than a menu word a server is asked about, so it does not belong on this roster.

A real menu heading, but Level II by the standard: common at good restaurants, not fine-dining vocabulary, and explained in one sentence (the house buys whole animals and serves every part, so expect offal and odd cuts under that heading). American menus print 'whole-animal' as often as 'nose-to-tail'. It belongs in a Level II pass beside Larder, not on this roster.

challenges.because: Not fine-dining-only vocabulary. Every Restaurant Week card, brunch prix fixe and bistro set menu in America prints "supplement 12" or "+15", so a Level II server meets it weekly, and the explanation is one sentence (an add-on charged on top, per person unless it says for the table). That is the Chef de Partie standard exactly: common at a good restaurant, needs a sentence. It is the right card to sit beside Prix Fixe (Level I) but it does not belong at Sous Chef.

It is printed on the last line of every tasting menu at every tasting-menu house and said at every table every night there, which is the definition of fine-dining vocabulary (Level III), not the rare word a senior server meets a few times a year (Level IV, beside Acquerello and Ballotine). It is one step past Amuse-Bouche (Level II) and takes one sentence: the tray of tiny sweets after dessert, included. Petits Fours belongs on the card as an alias since half the houses print that instead.

missing: Omakase [3]: the third menu structure after Prix Fixe and Tasting Menu, printed on the menu of every sushi counter and most Japanese-leaning fine dining; guests ask whether they choose anything, how many courses, and whether the price is fixed; not an alias of Tasting Menu (fd_0290 carries Degustation and Chef's Tasting only) and it behaves differently: ordered at the counter, sized by the chef, often priced by tier.

Biodynamic [3]: a sourcing claim printed on produce and on nearly every fine-dining wine list; guests ask if it means organic; the answer (a private Demeter standard, farm as one organism, organic and then some, lunar calendar, no federal meaning) takes more than a sentence; not in everyCard.

Line-Caught [3]: printed as "line-caught", "hook-and-line" or "pole-caught" on fish courses at fine dining; guests ask if it is the same as wild or day-boat; it is a method claim about how the fish was taken, not where or when, and sits above Wild-Caught (I) and Day-Boat (II) as the confusable third; not in everyCard.

Intermezzo [3]: the palate-cleanser course printed by name on tasting menus ("intermezzo: yuzu granita"); guests ask if it is dessert; not in everyCard (Granita fd_0257 is the food, not the course); one step past Amuse-Bouche (II) and the natural pair to Mignardises.

Chef de Cuisine [3]: the blurb says this section holds what the kitchen stations are called, and Garde Manger is its only card; "Chef de Cuisine" is printed at the foot of menus under the executive chef's name and guests ask who actually cooks tonight; the answer (the chef who runs this kitchen daily under a chef who may run several) is a sentence with a nuance; not in everyCard.

Nose-to-Tail [3]: a menu heading and sourcing claim at good and fine-dining houses ("whole-animal butchery", "nose-to-tail"); guests ask what they are committing to and whether the offal cards are in that section; a menu word, not a book word, and not in everyCard.
sections.note: Four proposed, the section's aim. Two more were weighed and held because guests ask about them less: Intermezzo (Level III, the palate-cleanser course printed on tasting menus) and Chef de Cuisine (Level III, the title at the foot of a fine-dining menu that guests confuse with Executive Chef); either fills a slot if the owner wants more menu-structure words. Rejected for the standard or for overlap: USDA Prime, Line-Caught, Foraged and Diver (honestly Level II); A5 (the Wagyu card already carries the grade); Omakase (too close to the Tasting Menu aliases); Grain-Finished (the Grass-Fed gist already covers finishing); Biodynamic (a wine-list word, Codex territory). Lexicon: no candidate covers these, so no slugs are given, but the Lexicon does hold "sashimi-grade-and-ikejime" (category Fish & Shellfish, below the candidate levels) which the Ikejime card's writer can anchor to if the owner allows an out-of-candidate link.

drop.because: The same word is proposed twice: methods has Koji-Aged at Level 4 and pantry has Koji at Level 4, and both cards would have to teach the same thing (rice grown with Aspergillus oryzae, enzymes that tenderize and build savor). Methods is the section whose blurb fits: menus print the verb form (Koji-Aged Ribeye, Koji-Cured Pork Collar, shio-koji-marinated) far more often than the bare noun, the guest's question is what was done to the food and how it differs from Dry-Aged, which is the methods blurb's 'tell the near neighbors apart', and koji is neither a vinegar, a pickle, a preserve nor 'a seasoning that finishes a plate'. Methods also held no Level IV card while pantry already holds three (Banyuls, Saba, Verjus). The methods card should carry Koji, Shio Koji and Koji-Cured as aliases so a study search on any form lands; the Miso card (fd_0280) can then point to it. Pantry keeps three sound Level III proposals.

move.because: Wrong by the standard's own signals. It is not rare: hazelnut or almond dacquoise is a stock component word on fine-dining plated-dessert cards, printed about as often as Crémeux and Sablé, which this roster places at Level 3. It explains in one sentence from a Level 1 card (Meringue, fd_0240): a nut meringue baked as a layer. The Level 4 peers named in the standard (Acquerello, Bottarga, Ballotine, Banyuls) are genuinely rarer and take longer to explain. The proposal's own motive, that the section held no Level IV card, is not a criterion of the standard, and its strongest point, a tree-nut allergen hidden behind a French word, argues for learning it earlier, not later; the standard's tie-breaker runs downward. Level 3 beside Pâte à Choux and Clafoutis.

critic.notes:
Verified against tools/deck/out/roster.methods.brief.json (everyCard, 281 cards), the per-section briefs, the source modules in tools/derive/floor-deck/*.mjs, and tools/deck/audit/levels.json.

DUPLICATES: none of the 56 proposed terms or their stated aliases is a card term or alias anywhere in everyCard, and a grep of the source modules confirms it. Several words appear only inside other cards' body text or menu lines, which supports rather than blocks them: the deck already prints Dover sole (preparations.mjs:300), foie gras torchon (bread.mjs:39, meats.mjs:107), bordelaise (cuts.mjs:21, sauces.mjs:42, :226), black garlic (mushrooms.mjs:21), Carolina Gold (cured.mjs:23, fish.mjs:40, :321), white truffle (starches.mjs:248) and bomba (starches.mjs:231) in its own lines and traps without teaching them. The one cross-section double is Koji / Koji-Aged, resolved above. White Truffle and Summer Truffle sit beside the Level 1 Truffle card (fd_0147), which contrasts white and black in half a sentence; neither is a term, alias or spelling variant, the Lexicon holds white-truffle as its own Level 4 entry, and the section blurb is 'what a truffle is and is not', so both stand. Chicken Oysters is not a variant of Oysters (fd_0115); it stands, though by blurb it is a poultry cut and reads more like cuts than meats ('small birds, game and the organ meats'); Duck Breast already living in meats is the precedent that lets it stay.

NO MENU PRINTS IT: none found. Teres Major, Nage, Regenerative and Triple Crème are printed under the forms the proposals name as aliases (Petite Tender/Bistro Filet; à la nage; regeneratively raised; triple cream), so their alias lists are load-bearing and must be written.

LEVELS: all other placements hold by the standard. Escolar at 4 stands on the wax-ester caution a senior server must deliver correctly; Bomba at 4 stands beside Freekeh and Farro Piccolo as a rare variety, though the roster's own Carolina Gold argument (variety = III, brand = IV) cuts against it and the owner may prefer 3. Vacherin at 4 stands on rarity alone.

FALSE PREMISES TO CORRECT BEFORE WRITING (not grounds to drop): Stracciatella's claim that the Burrata gist 'never names it' is wrong, Burrata's why (dairy.mjs:232) names stracciatella; Taleggio's claim that Washed Rind has 'no named example' is wrong, Washed Rind (dairy.mjs:314-315) names Taleggio twice, so the Taleggio card should be written as the example the style card already points to; Vacherin's claim that the deck holds Vacherin Mont d'Or 'under Washed Rind' is wrong, Washed Rind never mentions it, so the two-meanings point is a real-world confusable, not an in-deck one. The Foie Gras card (meats.mjs:107-110) already mentions torchon and carries lexiconSlug foie-gras-torchon-mi-cuit-and-ethics-of-service; the Torchon card should link to it.

LEXICON SLUGS: the candidates list is identical for every section (30 entries). White Truffle should carry slug white-truffle and Matsutake slug matsutake; neither proposal named its slug.
